utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Music. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Music. If you could tell the Court your full name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: My name is Mehmed Music.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Music, if you could move yourself forward towards the microphone, please, to assist the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: My name is Mehmed Music.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can have 65 ter 90229, please, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Music, what you'll see on the screen in front of you is a statement that was prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor that brought together the evidence you have previously provided to the Prosecution, to the Bosnian authorities, and to the Trial Chambers in the Slobodan Milosevic and Momcilo Krajisnik cases. Can you confirm that when you arrived in The Hague on Sunday, that an interpreter from the Prosecution read that statement to you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And after you made several corrections, can you confirm that you signed that statement on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And looking at the statement in front of you, is that your signature you see at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: There are two parts of your statement, Mr. Music, that I wish to clarify with you now. The first concerns the weapons or arms that were held by persons in Musici village prior to the takeover on 20 May, and for those in the courtroom I'm referring to paragraphs 15, 22, 25 and 31 of the statement. I'd just like to clarify this part of your evidence. You say in your statement that people in your village had hunting rifles. First, did you, in your household, have a hunting rifle or hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Did other persons, other households in the village that you knew of have what you describe as hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since my uncles, both of them are deceased, both of them got killed on that day, one of them had a weapon. He was a hunter and his younger son, too, who was killed in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You say that there were approximately 35 households in Musici. Are you able to estimate of those 35 households, how many had hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, we had three hunting rifles, and we had four police reservists who were on the reserve police force before the war as well. For quite a few years, five or six perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: When you refer to hunting rifles, Mr. Music, do you consider hunting rifles as automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And were there any automatic weapons in the village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: As I've already explained, the police had four Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, in your statement, you refer to an interrogation which occurred at the municipal building garage. This is in paragraph 47. And you said that they were particularly interested in the Browning that was left in the village. First, am I right in saying that a Browning is a machine-gun, Mr. Music?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: It was a Browning, but I hadn't seen it myself. As people were withdrawing, those who wanted to withdraw via Mount Igman, they brought that, say, about 300 metres away from my house in the woods, but I was questioned about that five times, mistreated and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Just to focus on this Browning that you later heard was in the village, do you know who obtained that Browning?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, it came from Binjezevo because people were withdrawing from Binjezevo, Mostar Raskrsce, Mesevici, it came from the police warehouse that was in Gladno Polje, that is to say between Mostar Raskrsce and Rakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And other than that one Browning, was there any other machine-gun or heavy weaponry in the village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: We had a machine-gun that was brought by the late Cedo Domuz, who was police commander at Mount Igman. Thanks to him perhaps, the people who did survive survived because the reserve police force and part of the police who were regular police and who were in the area of Tarcin and Pazarici, well, they went out to Mount Igman so thanks to them Igman was saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Let's just focus on this one machine-gun, Mr. Music. Do you know when it was obtained approximately?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, I remember in Kovacevici, when my late brother-in-law came to see me on the 8th of May, 1992, and Kovacevici was attacked on the 7th of May 1992, he came, and this is what he said to me, Father-in-law, this is not good. My brother was wounded last night and also a neighbour, Vatric. Let your daughters go. My two daughters were with me: Alma Music, born in 1973; and Ajla -- no, not Ajla, Amela, who was born on the 1st of November, 1979. They came -- I mean Cosic, Remzija came and Kadric, Dino, he was his best friend, best man at his wedding. They took my daughters to Hadzici. Somebody organised buses for the women and children to leave, so people were leaving on the 7th, 8th and 9th. Afterwards, no one could leave Hadzici. As for the Browning, it arrived between the 8th and 11th. Please don't take my word for the date because the 11th of May 1992, was the day when people were executed; that is to say, 12 Bosniaks and two Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And Mr. Music, do you remember the condition of that machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: It was from that other war, a very old one. It was among the old weaponry that was kept. As I've already said, in Gladno Polje between Rakovica and Mostar Raskrsce. Since Dzevad Music, my relative, was on the reserve police force and the late Cedo Domuz as well and yet another member of the police, the pre-war police, they came to see us, to see how we were doing, whether we were hanging on, whether we were guarding the village from Blazuj. As I've already said in my statement, already in 1991, paramilitaries arrived in Blazuj, Chetniks from Serbia and Montenegro. As I've already described --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Music --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there. I can assure you that everyone in the courtroom has your statement, and that will form part of your evidence, so if you could just concentrate on the specific questions in the assurance that your evidence is contained within this statement. The second part of your statement that I just wish to briefly clarify concerns your detention at the Hadzici sports and cultural centre. I'm referring to paragraph 57. And you say that on the second day of Bajram, Serb paramilitaries came to that centre. In your statement you describe them as Arkan's men. In statements you gave to Bosnian authorities in 2004 and 2005, you describe them as Seselj's men. Are you able to tell the Court how that discrepancy arises?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, they introduced themselves as Seselj's men. However, those who were guarding us said that they were Arkan's men. That is quite unclear to me what the truth is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Aside from those two clarifications, Mr. Music, can you confirm that the contents of this statement are accurate?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if I was to ask you today to describe the same events, you would provide the same information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I ask that this statement be admitted into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2403, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Music I'm now going to read a brief summary of your evidence for the benefit of the public following this trial. In 1992, Mr. Mehmed Music was living in Musici, a settlement of 35 Muslim households next to the village of Usivak. Beginning in April 1992, local Serb leaders began to ask Muslims in Musici to surrender their weapons. These demands intensified in May when, after the capture of Kovacevici on 11 May, Serb forces began to shoot at Musici. The village was shelled from 15 May. On 17 or 18 May, local Serb leaders again demanded that the Muslims surrender, telling them, "This is Serb land." Intense shelling resumed until the 20th of May when a Serb force of between 50 and 60 men took over the village by force, aided by two Praga tanks. Three Muslim men were killed and the witness and 13 others were detained. For five and a half months, starting from 20 May 1992, Mr. Music was detained at seven different locations, including the garage of the Hadzici municipal building, the Hadzici sports and cultural centre, the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks at Lukavica, the Kula prison and Planjo's house in Svrake, each of these locations listed in schedule C of the indictment in this case. Over this five and a half month period, Mr. Music was abused, beaten and humiliated, and, in turn, observed the ill treatment and beatings of other Muslim detainees. For example, while being detained in the garage at the Hadzici municipal building in May, Mr. Music and others were forced to load ammunition at a weapons storage facility and were barely fed. At the Hadzici sports and cultural centre, Serb paramilitaries forced detainees to sing Chetnik songs, detainees were chased and beaten, and in one instance, one detainee was forced to place his mouth on another man's penis. During his detention at barracks in Lukavica, Mr. Music was one of 48 men who were called out of a room. Those 48 men were forced to run a gauntlet of beatings to a room where three Serb military officers waited for them at a desk. When it transpired that Mr. Music had mistakenly responded to the call, he was returned. However, Mr. Music states that the 47 other men, which included his own brother, Miralem Music, were never seen again. He believes they were targeted because they had previously worked for the JNA in some capacity. Mr. Music was subject to several failed exchange attempts. On one occasion, the exchange failed because the Serb side wanted to exchange civilians in what was meant to be a one-for-one prisoner exchange. During these failed attempts, Mr. Music was again detained at the sports hall in Hadzici, this time along with 500 others, the majority of which were women, children and elderly. Mr. Music was finally exchanged on 5 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Music, there are two areas I wish to further briefly explore with you. In paragraph 15 of your statement and you're talking here about activities prior to the takeover of your village, you state: "I think that the main command for the area was in Todorovic's house." And you're referring to Gavro Todorovic. Do you know if Mr. Todorovic was a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: He belonged to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I know that for several reasons, because I was following the accused, I cannot refer to him as a gentleman, for me he is a criminal, when he came to Raco -- Ratko, well, the main mentor in Hadzici was the church, that was headed by Milan Lucic. Drago Milosevic, who was the director of Ingrap, then Aco Lubura, unfortunately I was so surprised to see that even a teacher could turn out to be like that, also Ratko Radic, where these meetings were organised, because the said accused came to Hadzici, about 15 times, as far as I know, because I have one of my fields there where they met, it's about 60 metres away from there as the crow flies, so I had the opportunity of seeing the accused servicing his car at Ratko Radic's. He had it painted. This was just a trick so that people would not get suspicious that he was coming for that other reason. Ratko Radic was also president of the municipality at the time, and they were the ones who were in decision-making positions. Whatever they organised was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And Mr. Music, sorry if I can just focus you on Mr. Todorovic and how you know that he was a member of the SDS, Mr. Todorovic from your village.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, since we were neighbours, we visited each other on different -- on the occasion of different holidays. He came to me for Bajram and I visited him when they had their holidays. Until then, I did not distinguish between people, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Roma, everybody was the same to me. I viewed people individually, not as criminals. However, unfortunately, it was the 2nd or 3rd of August 1991, Meho is my nickname, my real name is Mehmed, and that actually saved my life in Lukavica. He said, Meho, well, you know, we had this joint cistern. The Serbs and us shared it. He said, Don't go up there. And I said, Why? And he said, Serbs were up there. And they were up there. They were walking around there. It is because above Pusara, Usivak, Genge [phoen], in a pine wood, that is where they had their command. We found it when we entered Hadzici on the 6th of March, 1992. They had between 35 and 40 beds there, double bunk beds. They brought some camp inmates there to work for them, to dig trenches, dugouts, whatever. However, I only had my shed left. Everything else they had burned down so there were only two houses that remained. In the meantime, one of them had burned down just before the night when we came in. So I know because of that, Gavro told me. I knew everything, I knew hardly -- there was hardly any neighbour who was not a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. The second issue, Mr. Music, relates to testimony you've given about your detention, again at the sports hall. This is the first time you were detained there in June 1992. And you say at paragraph 65 that you were told that you were going to be exchanged and the men were all put on buses, four buses, in the evening, and you say that they allowed the women, children and three men to stay behind. Can you recall approximately how many of the people detained at the sports hall at that time were women or children?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, there were 283 of us camp inmates. I cannot tell you about women and children because women and children came on that day when they were clearing the compound in this hamlet called Kucice and then everybody, women, children, 90 year old men, I mean they did not ask any questions, they were not human beings, they were animals. I mean, the way they behaved, if I tell you that a person did not have his legs, can you imagine what had happened? So three buses remained parked in front of the sports hall and we went in. Before leaving, the people started embracing those guards and they were pleased to be going for an exchange. They said you're going to be Kobiljaca, Kiseljak, and I sort of thought, Oh, you poor fools, how can you be so happy? There is no way they are going to let us go because if they do let us go they are going to have 282 persons against them. That was not in their interests. Their only interest was for them to survive, nobody mattered. Nobody else mattered, Croats, Roma, nobody. It was only important for them to have all Serbs in one state. This never came to be, and it never will happen. Then we went opposite the police -- or rather the post office, that's where the municipality of Hadzici was. Four men walked into my bus. Believe me they smelled so bad that they didn't have any opportunity to bathe. They didn't give us water, anything. They would give us a single bottle of water, 48 men. There was no air. There was this metal door and there was hardly any air. When it would rain, we would take off our T-shirts and we would try to wipe our bodies. They took me prisoner when I was wearing boots, you see, so I was so embarrassed I couldn't take off those boots, and I asked them whether they would let me go and wash my feet and they said, No way, "balija," you're not going to need that and all that was done by the locals, it was done by the police, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt you, sir. I must remind you that your evidence is before the Judges in the form of this statement, they do have it and now that it's been admitted into evidence, we'll read that. It's difficult that you can't retell your story in total today but as we discussed prior to your testimony, that's a function of this Court. So I appreciate your understanding of that. Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness. There are just four associated exhibits, two of those have already been admitted since the filing of the notification. That's 65 ter 01449, which is now P2328, and 65 ter 01439, which is P2298. The other two are yet to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which are photograph and map?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those will be admitted. Let's give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 01440 will be Exhibit P2404, and 65 ter 20798 will be Exhibit P2405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Music, you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic, who is entitled to cross-examine your evidence. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could just note for the record that we were informed by the Prosecution that this witness had testified in four separate trials in Bosnia, two in the State Court of Bosnia for the cases of Rade Veselinovic and Wardens Lalovic and Skijevic [phoen] and two instances in the Cantonal Court in Sarajevo for Nemanja Jovicic, Momir Covic and Vlastimir Pusara, and also another case involving Boro Krsmanovic. And we don't have any of those transcripts, and, again, if we receive them and they contain something important, we will let you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Music.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Please do not refer to me as mister. In your eyes I'm a "balija."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear me using the word "balija?"

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I have heard quite a few of your lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear me use the word "balija?"

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I had been humiliated by the people under you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The only superior entity to me was God and he never referred to you as "balija."

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You don't believe in God.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave this subject. I'm going to refer to you as mister but you can consider yourself whatever you wish. In your village, you organised patrols and guards.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: We organised patrols and guard duty because the paramilitary formations, the Chetniks who had beard were there. You can't have a proper soldier who is between 35 and 50 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, in order for us not to stay here for a whole week, could you kindly answer my questions with a yes or a no whenever possible? I wanted to ask you this: You said that -- shall I call up your statement that you gave in 2002 in order to remind you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: If necessary, I can be at your disposal for five days.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we have 65 ter 9153.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today, on page 5, line 13 and onwards, you said that in 1991, Chetniks came to your area. Was there in 1991 at least some semblance of authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic used to declare himself a Serb but he wasn't a Serb. Was he in power in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you know when the referendum and everything else took place. He was a gentleman and I'm honoured to have had him as a president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at page 2. Today you said that Chetniks came. However, in this statement, you said that way back in August 1991, you noticed that reservists had arrived. Now, look at page 2, please, after the words "Coca-Cola": "Before the beginning of the war in our region, already in August 1991, I noticed that reservists had arrived," and so on and so forth. Let's clarify this right now. When you say Chetniks, were you referring to a particular formation or were you referring to the Serbs in general?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No. There were quite a few honest Serbs, and vice versa, there are some people of good standing in my nation as well, who did not deserve to be called names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me who came in 1991? Was it the Chetniks or the JNA reservists?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I claim that those were Chetniks dressed in JNA uniforms. It was not the JNA. That was the Serbian army, and I really regret to have served in the army in Nis which apparently is in another state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, we are hearing you through interpretation. The interpreters' interpretation. If you could put a pause before you start answering the question. Thank you very much. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this 2002 statement of yours, you did not say that those were Chetniks but, rather, that reservists came, and you also say that they did not behave as the JNA army, and you say that you were afraid of their incursion into the village overnight, the villagers posted guards during the night. Now, let's try to make this more precise. You say that in August of 1991, it was not the JNA reservists who came but rather that they were Chetniks. You say here that they were actually reservists but that you did not like their behaviour. Was there any state authority in power in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991, and was this occurrence the subject of an investigation? Could that be considered a major event, the arrival of Chetniks in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: As I already told you a minute ago, I can tell you with full responsibility that towards the end of August, not the beginning of August, between 30th of August and the 6th of September, because that's the time when my daughters had their academic year starting, we saw a man with an automatic rifle, he had a pistol, and he was entering and mapping something on the map. So he was marking the main elevations where -- which were later used for Praga and mortar emplacements. I was observing all of this through my binoculars because we have about 60 acres of land, and a few houses there. So there is less than 500 metres to Radic's house where you held meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Music, we only have two hours for this cross-examination. I don't want to detain you any longer, and please focus. I'm going, on the other hand, to skip a number of questions. You said here in your 1997 statement, as follows: "At the beginning of the year, we organised patrols in order to protect our women and children. Nobody did us any harm but those people were getting drunk and we could hear them singing Chetnik songs." If you would like, I could call up this statement of yours.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: What you quoted is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, briefly, what do you consider to be Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, look, you know when Ravno in Herzegovina was razed to the ground that's when the war in Herzegovina started and they were singing the village of Ravno would be flattened. They said, Kill "balija," they swore at "balija." So this was less than 100 metres, as the crow flies, from my property. We could hear people getting drunk on cheap brandy and then they became brave and started firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time, nearly all the Muslims, generals, colonels, lieutenant-generals, and majors remained in the JNA? We had Vehbija Karic, the commander of the 2nd District, and that Enver Hadzihasanovic commanded a tank brigade; in other words, the Muslims were still in the JNA at the time. Nevertheless, you claim that this was not the JNA but the Chetniks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Look, you are full of lies. Let me deny what you said. The son of my brother-in-law was a non-commissioned officer in the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks. I'm not going to tell you the name of the officers who told our young men, children, The war is in the offing, try to get out as -- in any way you can. So sometime in September, he left. He even risked being sanctioned, but he left nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no time to go into details. Now, tell me, in your amalgamated statement, on page 4, paragraph 15, you say, and I have to read it in English because the interpreters will translate this better. So towards the end of paragraph 15: [In English] "There were about 35 of us who had organised our search to patrol and we continued guarding the houses. We had only our own weapons, which were just our old hunting weapons. We had no military weapons. [Interpretation] Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Commander? Omer Alic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, in paragraph 31, of your statement, on page 6, I have to read it again in English: [In English] "Chetniks came into Musici from all sides. They were supported by Pragas. We had two or three hunting guns, perhaps somebody had a pistol, that's all." [Interpretation] This is the weapons that you possessed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, look, you said the 28th of May. That's not correct. That was the 20th of May. I know when my uncles were killed, and I know when I was picked up. So don't twist the facts and tell lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I read out 20th.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: But you said the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's look at your 1995 statement, which is 65 ter 8978, pages 2, both in the English and the Serbian. You said: "Through members of the reserve police force, we managed to obtain some weapons in order to try and put up some resistance"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: In my previous testimony, I said that four of my relatives were in the reserve police force, and then, between the 7th and 10th, the late Cedo Domuz came, and you know very well that he was a true gentleman, a commander, and his family is enjoying more rights than any Bosnian -- Bosniak officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was not only the reserve police that had weapons, but they also provided you with the weapons because you say here, through members of the reserve police force, we managed to procure a number of weapons. Is this what you said in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: At that time, they brought one old M-53 submachine-gun. The late Cedo Domuz gave us his own hand gun. He gave it to a relative of mine. So that was his own gun. When we he were chased, and you will have an opportunity to hear who it was who captured me, Rade Veselinovic was chasing Selim Music, forcing him to run because he had lost this weapon. They were firing at us from guns and Pragas in order to create mayhem in the village because only women and children were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at your 2005 statement. I'm going to read out and if you disagree, we can call it up on our screens. So that's page 3 in the Serbian and page 4 in the English. Well, let's look at this paragraph. It's 1D3361. 1D3361. Page 3 in Serbian and page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to read it out to you. You speak about hunting rifles and carbines. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, is a carbine a hunting rifle which uses 7.9 millimetre ammunition just like M-48 rifles?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that it can be both a military and civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now you say: "There were also members of the reserve police who had weapons issued to them. Through members of the reserve policemen, we managed to obtain some weapons." So some weapons is definitely more than one piece of weapon, one submachine-gun; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, look, you are really going to extremes here. Whatever I said here, I stand by it, and what were we able to do with our rifles against Pragas and guns?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Except for what you said, did you have any other weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement, the same one, page 4 in the Serbian, and English page 5, you say: "They found a hand grenade on me and some ammunition, and they confiscated it from me." Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Earlier, you said that you didn't see that machine-gun but now in the cross-examination, you said that the machine-gun did come to the village after all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After all the things that we said here, it seems that paragraphs 15 and 31 of your consolidated statement are not quite correct; is that correct? It wasn't just two or three hunting rifles, there were hand grenades, machine-guns and automatic weapons, too.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, if you continue like that, it will turn out that we also had tanks and guns, cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you said that a machine-gun was lost, that it wasn't hidden in the village, and that you knew that, you stated that, it was a Browning, it's a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Please believe me, I didn't see that, Your Honours, I guarantee that with my life. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that it was hidden or that it was lost? What is your position on that now?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I heard that people brought it to the woods, between Radic's house and my field, Radic's house where you had the meetings. Nobody from my village saw it, those who were withdrawing from the Raskrsce, Mesevici, a part of Rakovica, people were fleeing to save their lives. However, they kept ending up at Igman. I am working as the president of the missing persons commission, and I was looking for 235 persons since that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Unfortunately, I wish we had more time. We would gladly discuss that as well. How did the Serbs react to your spying and observing the behaviour of the Serbs in Hadzici, the Chetniks, as you refer to them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Once when we were on guard duty, we saw Rade Marilovic, that's my neighbour, and another person called Rade Nesren. We stopped him near the house of Gavro Todorovic. They were transporting weapons. This was not being hidden at all. Because I don't know if you know that, I told that to the Prosecutor. We were not working in the Coca-Cola. It was hit by the shell. It was a guy called Mehmed Residovic. We were not working, so we were just walking around, also Vasilije Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, so let's leave that for another occasion. You said in your consolidated statement, paragraph 8, that after the elections in 1991, I'm going to read it in English: [In English] "After the 1991 elections, I used to go out into the field and followed the movement of my Chetnik neighbours." [Interpretation] You were not observing people who were coming in. You were observing your Serbs, the neighbours, to whom you refer as your Chetnik neighbours. How did they feel about you looking at what they were doing through binoculars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Music, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Hasn't been established that the Serb neighbours knew they were being observed, and, therefore, couldn't possibly know how they felt about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the witness would be able to answer the question. Yes, Mr. Music?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you want me to go into details, after that, in the month of September, but don't hold me to the date, please, I saw below Igman a chopper landing in the fields and when they were unloading boxes of ammunition, that was where the front line was. So just like the Prosecutor said, they were not able to see me. I was watching from the woods. I'm not so silly as to go into the meadow. I used to be in the so-called JNA, it was the Serbian army, but I was a corporal and I was in the reserve forces as well. Towards the end we all had to return our uniforms, because us Muslims were no longer required there. That much I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have given 15 statements and testified that many times so far, you didn't say that your neighbours, the Serbs, had a chopper in 1991 and were unloading anything. Are you talking about the Yugoslav People's Army, which in 1991 was the legal, accepted force, it co-operated with Izetbegovic, or are you speaking about your neighbours, Serbs, who were flying around loading, unloading and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, it wasn't the Yugoslav People's Army. It was the Serbian army. I state that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can we now look at your statement from 1993. This is 65 ter 22205, page 2 in the English and the Serbian. We can read it. We don't even have to call it up if you confirm it. You say: "Informative talks with me were conducted by Mijatovic, Veka, Rade Veselinovic and Zoran Gasevic. They were also interested in the following questions, and in particular, in the Browning that remained hidden in the village." So you knew that it was hidden in the village, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, why don't you give the full first and last names? You appointed the people who were in the criminal investigations police: Brane Mijatovic, called Veka, his nickname is Veka; Zoran Gasevic, son Ratko, his father worked with me together for 15 years. Thanks to his father, and you might have the opportunity to find all the things that I said about that, thanks to his father, who knew that I had a large sum of money but I didn't dare offer it to anyone, I stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to stick to the questions in your answers. In 1991 -- sorry, in 1992, sometime in April, did you dig trenches in your village, as it states in paragraph 16 of your consolidated statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: We didn't dig trenches in the village. We had two false ones and a proper one. This was in order to hold back people. We dug out the trenches, some 200 or 300 metres from my house where the woods were so that they could see them, and these were not proper, real trenches. We would just walk up and down. It was a kind of deception, in the third one. They kept shelling so much that they were knocking down the trees. You did the same thing in Poljine but there was nobody there in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. They were shelling? --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After this answer, as indicated, we will take a break for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the Trial Chamber to review the decision again, not only because of the voluminous answers by the witness but also in view of the 15 statements given by this witness on various occasions? I would, based on that, kindly request more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I'm not minded to give another extension. We will discuss it. We will take a break for 15 minutes. --- Break taken at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: There is a correction I need to make to the associated exhibits. Photograph which was Exhibit P409 referred to in paragraph 45 is, in fact, 65 ter 01438, and that has not been admitted. I indicated before that that photograph had been previously admitted under an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's then give that a separate number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2406, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, when answering the question, please try to answer directly and be concise as much as possible, please. Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 to 21 of your consolidated statement, you described the events in the village of Kovacevici. Is it correct that you don't have a direct experience of these events?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I do have knowledge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Direct knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, because this is where my daughter's husband, my son-in-law, was killed, his brother, his nine nephews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Redzo Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at your statement from 1996? This is 1D3358. 1D3358. Serbian page 2, English page 3. Let's wait till it appears, and there you say, and now I can emphasise this is not the beginning of the paragraph, but the middle of it, "I can say that" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the accused to let us know where he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, unless you identify to us where -- from where you are reading, the interpreters find it -- would find it very difficult to interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just going to find it now in the Serbian. It's in the middle of the page, in the Serbian, "In my previous statement ...," that's what it says. Let's see if we can see it in the English as well. In the English, it should be page 3. In the last third of the page in the English, in the middle, it says, "In my earlier statement ..." In the English it begins with the words, [In English] "I can now emphasise ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So: "In my previous statement, I said that the attack on our village of Musici ...," and so on and so forth, "and now I can emphasise that before the attack on Musici, the attack on Kovacevici had taken place on the 10th or 11th of May of 1992 on which occasion there were many casualties among the local people from this village. I was not present on that occasion and I cannot say anything about those details." Did you state this in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. But since the late Suljo Kovacevic, who lost two sons on that occasion, two brothers, and four nephews, was in the commission with me after he left the camp in late October 1992, I was in the exchange commission, I think you probably had time to look at that, and he told me that in that operation, the person in command was Tihomir Glavas because he was the chief of police at the time and there was this Crisis Staff, so Slobodan Avlijas, judge, the judge, is the most involved in that incident because he did what he did, and perhaps the Judges can give you some more information about that information that I discovered in 2004. He told me everything down to the last detail. He was brought in when I was in the camp. I was transferred to the sports hall on the 25th, Suljo was brought in on the 27th or the 28th, I'm not sure of the date and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. But you never mentioned in any of your previous statements that it was Tihomir Glavas and Judge Avlijas were in charge of that attack. Was that some kind of legitimate raid?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, there was Tihomir Glavas, from the SDS, like Nemanja Jovicic, Rade Veselinovic from Vojkovici, to Momo Ilic from Blazuj. They executed them in front of the culture hall in Hadzici. There were 12 Bosniaks, two Croats, and they carried out this genocide against them twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you there? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Probably they would have called me to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you were not there and you didn't see that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 of the consolidated statement, you say that during the alleged attack on your village of Musici, women and children, including your wife, were together with you in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify for me exactly what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 36, second sentence: [In English] "Women and children, including my wife, stayed behind." [Interpretation] Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. But a number of the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the rest of the women and children? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They left on May 8th, 1992, when buses were organised to go to the liberated territory towards Pazarici, Starici, Konjic, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, you evacuated most of the women and children from the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, to prevent them from becoming casualties like the ones who stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So who was a casualty before the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, we had the opportunity to see what Tintor was doing in Svrake and Foca. You had two corps there were Montenegro, the Niksic Corps was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we have enough now. I'm interested in what you know and what you saw. You stated that in your statement of 2007, page 6, towards the end, you say how you were interrogated, and you say: "They were interested why we had sent the women and children away." The Serbs wanted to know why you had sent the women and children away. And they believed that you were preparing something; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. They asked you, though, why you sent the women and children away?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I didn't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at your statement 1D3360 from 2007, page 4 in the Serbian, page 5 in the English. It says here, at the top: "Everything was happening quickly and I already had no time to think, and my wife asked me what I -- what did I think if I left -- sent my kids with them; that is, with the daughter who was living in the Hercegovacka Street. So there were buses organised for the elderly and the children and they left for Pazaric and Tarcin." What was it that was unfolding quickly before the 8th of May, Mr. Music, so that you had to evacuate your family, the women and children to Pazaric and Tarcin?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: All right, I'm going to tell you. When my son-in-law told me that his brother was wounded and that this neighbour of his, too, Vatric, I went to the 12 Hercegovacka. There is a settlement called Kovacevici behind the municipality and most of the Kovacevic families were settled there, and returning from there across the bridge, I saw a colleague of mine called Pandurevic who worked with me. I didn't have the opportunity ever to say hello to him before that. His name was Bozidar Pandurevic. He had a playground for table tennis, but you all don't need to hear this from me. You know that better than I do. So he was walking on one side and then as soon as he saw me, he crossed over to the other side without greeting me, as if I was an alien or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Mr. Music, you sent your family, or, rather, civilians away from your village before the events of Musici because Musici happened on the 10th and 11th of May, whereas -- sorry, Kovacevici was on the 10th and 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Kovacevici, yes. But the first Kovacevici -- attack on Kovacevici - let me correct you - was on the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you evacuated your family on time because you planned an armed struggle. And from that point of view, the amalgamated statement is not correct that your women and children stayed behind you in the village; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You are full of lies, let me put it that way. There were about ten women and children left there. There is no reason for me to lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But your daughters?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Daughters, yes. I stated that and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 22 of your consolidated statement, you say that you stayed in the village and you refused the proposal to disarm, and that is what the Serbs offered to you, and you mentioned as a reason for refusing to disarm, this is what you say in paragraph 26: [In English] "We did not want to surrender, because by that time we had seen the surrender of people from Svrake on the TV and we knew that would -- what would happen to us." [Interpretation] That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I explain why we sent our women and children out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. We've dealt with that already.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already said that. Did the Serbs ask for you to surrender or to surrender your weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: To surrender and to surrender our weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you talk about the surrender anywhere before? You only talked about handing over weapons.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, in order to hand over weapons, we would have signed our very own death warrant in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This amalgamated statement seems to be missing something, because you said something different beforehand. Look at your statement of 2004, 65 ter 22213. 22213 is the 65 ter number. It is page 3 in Serbian, page 4 in English. Let us not wait. I'm going to read it out. This is what you say: "However, knowing what the fate of the Muslim population had been in the territory of the village of Ahatovici, Svrake, as well as other villages that had surrendered their weapons to the Serbs, we decided not to hand over our weapons," and so on and so forth. So it wasn't the Serbs -- that the Serbs were asking to you surrender, they were asking you to surrender your weapons. And secondly, you mentioned the village of Ahatovici; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because I had some family there in Ahatovici, so I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come you knew what the fate of Ahatovici was before May 1992 when the fighting in Ahatovici took place on the 29th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, look. We were following TV and radio and some people had access to telephones as well, so we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the 20th of May, a television broadcast said that Ahatovici would surrender weapons and that Serbs were fighting against them, right, 10 days in advance?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. If you know about everything, why are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did someone from the OTP or someone else suggest to you that you get rid of Ahatovici in your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by that, namely, that Ahatovici and Svrake handed over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a rank in the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, of a sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this organisation of yours, the Defence organisation of the village, did you hold a rank there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No. In case something happened, I was supposed to evacuate civilians, women, children and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about your house? Did it have an important role?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, women and children and everybody were hiding in my house because my house had three walls, and about a metre away from the house there was another wall. So if there were to be shelling, a shell could not pierce three walls so that's why people were seeking shelter there because my house is on the side, as it were, I mean, I had that house, it was there before but it was razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was guarded as well, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Nobody guarded it. Had someone guarded it, believe me, nobody would have barged into my house, or if I had weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters and to Judge Lattanzi because of this rush, but it is this threat of a lack of time that makes me nervous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at your consolidated statement, paragraph 33. Today, you said that you were arrested when you were in the shed and that you were wearing boots; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: If you have everything in front of you, I describe that extensively, that I went to Donji Hadzici. We heard that Kovacevici had been set on fire, there was different information coming in. And since I had cattle, I went to the shed so I was wearing boots because I was walking through the woods, we didn't dare risk being seen by the Chetniks. However, a sniper targeted us at Majdan, as you know, opposite Radic's house. You were there several times. You know about all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just tell us where you were arrested, in the shed, outside, where?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: In my very own house. I went from the collection point where we organised the guards, that is the house of my late uncle, Music, and my brother-in-law was there having coffee. He arrived before me. You know what a brother-in-law is. My sister-in-law's husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Bosnians, Muslims and others do not enter houses wearing boots and do not have coffee wearing boots; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, look, you are lying all the time. This is very extreme what you're saying. Of course, I do not walk into the house wearing boots but I had to wear something when I walked out of the house because I prayed to the dear Allah, I would not allow anyone to enter my house that way. You know that we pray five times a day and things like that. I mean there is no reason for me he to explain all of that to you. But when Tomo Kovac -- I mean, Tomo Elcic and Mile Elcic, when they took me prisoner, I had to put some footwear on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you chose boots?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Oh, my goodness, if I knew that I was going to be paraded, if I was going to a party, I would have worn something different. If they forced you to leave wearing a T-shirt, that would be it. They said that they would take you away just so that they could loot your house. You were not waging war, you were looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you did not have any guards in front of yours house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: The guards were supposed to be opposite Usivak, 100 metres away. The late Ismet Music was supposed to be standing guard. He was not fit for the military, his eye sight was very poor. They set him on fire alive in Mucibare [phoen] in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is not contained in any one of your statements. Let us look at your statements.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You'll see it later. Have a close look at my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All of you favoured witnesses of the Office of the Prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this Office of the Prosecutor, you're memory gets better and better as time goes by. So let's have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's a totally unacceptable statement on your part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have time. I would like to ask the witness why he did not describe that kind of thing happening, that a man was set on fire alive and he said that's going to happen later. As time goes by he remembers more and more. All right. Let us look at paragraph 33: [In English] "I was sitting down and about to have a coffee when two Chetniks came in: Elcic, Tomislav; Elcic, Milan. They were members of the Serbian forces -- military police under the command of Veselinovic, Rade and Pusara, Dragan. They were supposed to have been guards at my house, but they must have [indiscernible] because I was very surprised to see those two come in." [Interpretation] For some reason, your house was supposed to be guarded by guards who had not done their job, and these people just barged into your house. Was your house some kind of headquarters or a place where preparations were carried out for combat? Yes or no? Just say yes or no. If it's no, just say so.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, look, I mean, you're really being very extreme. Why are you in such a hurry? You're going to stay on here for a long time. God willing, you're going to end up like your mentor, Milosevic, so what's the hurry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have no remarks in view of your hatred, sir. I'm just talking about your answers that are too lengthy. So in paragraph 38 of your consolidated statement, can we have the next page, please? There is what you said: [In English] "They brought other men from the settlement. Until we were 14, including me, they lined us all up next to Music, Alija's house." [Interpretation] Further down: [In English] "It's there that I saw the dead bodies of Music, Alija; Music, Dervis; and Music, Fadil. They were covered with blankets, but I knew who they were from their shoes and clothes." [Interpretation] Who killed these people who were covered with the blanket? How did they lose their lives?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably committed suicide. They were terrified of you Chetniks. A hand grenade was thrown in from the other side, from Radic's house, and further on, they were taken out towards Blazuj. So at that moment my late uncle, Alija, Music, and Music, Dervis, a relative of mine, and Fadil Music, they were there at that moment. Unfortunately, they were executed in Lukavica. These two men were by the wall, one was in one corner and the other one was in another corner. So one of them was just grazed on the head by this shrapnel. Actually, Nijaz Music, my cousin, was so terrified because this gunfire was there and they were using fragmentation bullets, and that is prohibited. I mean they are not human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You haven't said that before. Tell us about these people, were they killed in combat or were they killed as such?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They were executed in Lukavica. What do you mean combat? They went through the garage, and then in Lukavica on the 23rd in the morning, they were taken away and executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are talking about Musici but these two as well, were they killed in combat? Did they die in combat? Did they die in combat or were they killed in a situation that had nothing to do with combat?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They did put up a fight until this old submachine-gun got stuck. I told you that it was old weapons. And that was it. But if you have 50 well-armed men and Pragas --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 22205. Could we have that 65 ter number? 22205, page 2 in Serbian and page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they used that submachine-gun while they could use it, while they could use it to shoot, and then they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what you say. It's towards the top in Serbian and towards the top of the page in English as well, line 4 or 5. This is what it says: "I heard from other villagers that Alija, Dervis and Fadil Music had been killed by the Chetniks because Nemanja Jovicic and Marinko Djukanovic had thrown a hand grenade into a garage from which the aforementioned three had been offering resistance." So this description of the way in which these people lost their lives, that is not contained in the amalgamated statement; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: It is as you have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this a different submachine-gun or the one that was hidden in the forest?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the forest, I've explained it to you once already. You're not a child, not to be able to explain. No one saw it -- nobody from the village. There is a difference between a Browning and a submachine-gun. Do not pretend to be naive. You know better than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the fighting in your village, as you say in paragraph 43 of your amalgamated statement, together with the other fighters, you were taken prisoner and taken to Hadzici. You were locked up in a school there and you only spent ten minutes there.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: It wasn't ten minutes. It was about half an hour. And it seemed like an eternity to me. We were supposed to get killed there. Because they had a police unit there in that school and that's what I found out only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at this same document, in Serbian page 2, and as for English, please go back to page 2. There is a reference to Selim Music, Izil Behari [phoen], Idriz and Durmirsevic [phoen], so in the English version we will be able to find it. This is what it says: "Those of us who had been captured were escorted to the primary school in Hadzici. Miljenko and his brother Nedriko [phoen] Milosevic guarded us at the school. Ten minutes later, we were taken to the garage of the Hadzici Municipal Assembly. It's between the second and the third of the page in Serbian, and in English it's probably -- well, any way, you spent ten minutes there.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You are lying. I said that it was half an hour, and it seemed like an eternity to me. And let me explain this. They were not cuddling us over there, they started tearing these curtains like the one that you see over there and they were swearing at us, cursing our "balija" mothers, Ilija -- Alija can -- wants a state, right? And there was this child who hadn't even done his military service by then. He fainted because he saw what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we are restricting ourselves only to the amounts of time you spent at the school.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: About half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the 1993 statement, you said about ten minutes. Now, let's see what happened next after this ten minutes or half an hour as stated in your amalgamated statement. You were taken to the garage of the Hadzici municipal building where you were interrogated and where nobody mistreated you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't mention the two people that we found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. After six days in the garage you were transferred at the school centre in Hadzici where there were about 60 men and one woman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: That woman spent four years in prison with your female mentor, Radojka Pandurevic. She was with you in the SDS and on many occasions, since I worked at Coca-Cola factory for 10 or 15 hours a day. I used to see her car and her husband because she was working at Mostarska and Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to this. Now, let's see, you said, first of all, that they were Arkan's men and then you said that they were Seselj's men. You said that they introduced themselves as Seselj's men and somebody else told you that they were Arkan's men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You actually don't know who these people were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I saw them as aggressors. I didn't care whether they were Arkan's or Seselj's men. They were the same scum of the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 58 of your amalgamated statement, you talk about alleged maltreatment so we can look at paragraph 58: [In English] "I recognised her ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "I saw her take the pants off one man and saw her tell another man to suck the first man's sexual organ. They had to do it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In order to refresh your memory, can I tell you what you stated in 1993 when your memory of this dramatic event was much better? Now, let's look whether you said the same thing in 1993. The transcript is wrong. When you gave your first statement in 1993, and it only makes sense that at that time, your memory was better, you never described this dramatic event; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I can write two whole books. I do not wish to remember this very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have two statements, the first one almost immediately, 1993, this dramatic and drastic event was not described by you, was it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Listen, there were some things that made me embarrassed and I kept quiet about them, and I would never include them in my statements so don't be surprised because the things that you do was something that I was not always able to mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, look at paragraph 59 of your amalgamated statement: [In English] " I did not mention this incident in my first statement because these men, a neighbour of mine, was still alive. I was worried about that it would look like if I -- what it would look like if I speak about it." [Interpretation] Not now, again, you -- you did not give us his name actually, and you didn't think it was important at the time.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anyone suggest to you to insert this statement and to give this explanation and who did that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I was dictated by my clear conscience because I still meet this person occasionally. I might be more embarrassed about the whole thing than he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that several things are being repeated in the statements given by many statements, it seems that from Abu Ghraib detention to Hadzici, there is always someone who would like to play with people's genitalia. How is it possible that you're all telling one and the same story?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I'm not surprised that your lies. I remember what you said in 1991 at the Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave this aside. You are describing a drastic scene in your consolidated statement and you are not mentioning it in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I made a solemn declaration here and I stand by everything I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you -- your stay in the sports centre, you and the other imprisoned combatants were moved to Lukavica, whereas the women and children remained in Hadzici; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were taken prisoners, did the Serbs confiscate from you all the valuables?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Money, gold, they also took our ID cards, maybe their plan was when once they killed us we would not be identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now look what you say in paragraph 68 of your amalgamated statement. The next page: [In English] "We came in front of the gate to Kula prison."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "I had a watch on at the time. So I saw that it was about midnight or 15 minutes before the midnight." [Interpretation] Before you arrived in Kula, you had a watch?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I kept it hidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the sports centre in Hadzici, you were transferred to Lukavica where allegedly you were beaten by men dressed similarly to those at the sports hall in Hadzici; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Momo Mandic did not allow us to enter Kula but he ordered us to be taken to Lukavica. They unloaded us in Lukavica where the gym is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why wasn't this mentioned in any of your 15-odd statements?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Look, everything was happening so spontaneously, I actually never believed that I would survive because I -- I'm the only member of my family who had survived detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let us look at paragraph 86 of your amalgamated statement. It's next page or the one after that: [In English] "The ones who beat us now were wearing the same gloves as those who had beat us in the sports hall. Their hands were dirty, they carried big knives, and had beards," so on and so forth. [Interpretation] Is this a description of the people who beat you both in the sports centre in Hadzici and in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: And they had suffered enormous losses in Dobrinja, and due to that, they would barge into the buses and say, Look at "balijas," they have ammunition. I clearly remember that they burned cigarette on the neck of Meho Isic, a neighbour of mine. My father-in-law, an elderly man, was all covered in blood because he was beaten on the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's stick to your statements. Now you said that regular soldiers appeared and stopped these people; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's move to the next paragraph: [In English] "Regular JNA soldiers came in and told us to stop singing and asked us who had told us to do it? They told us no one would touch us any more. With this, the JNA soldiers brought us some food. [Interpretation] You were singing something, or you had been forced to sing, and but the soldier told you that you did not have to do that, that no one must touch you and they brought you food.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, let's call it army but they were actually the Serbian army. They were at the door and if he wanted to stop it, he would have stopped it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it what you said in this statement; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this happened towards the end of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: That happened on the 23rd of June. Forty-seven people's names were called out, including myself, which makes it 48. So you are skipping lots of things. Unlike you, I have enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that it was a rather hot day and that you had to take off your T-shirts to wipe your sweat off.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: That was while I was in the garage in Hadzici, but then, on the 23rd, we were forced to go to the toilet in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we are talking about the weather. Was it hot on the 23rd of June and on the following days, as you described?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I said you're skipping things. When we were taken prisoner I said that that was the situation in the garage. I didn't describe the situation in Lukavica as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After 23rd of June, is it -- was it hot in Sarajevo? Are summers hot in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you cannot say exactly that. There was some rain as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that you had a sweaters and jackets on.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No. I had a jacket but once your name is called out for beating, some of the people were only in T-shirts and they borrowed sweaters and jackets from their fellow inmates in order to alleviate the pain from being beaten by rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were 280 of you. Where were you put up?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: On the first night when we arrived, they maltreated us from 1.00 until probably 3.00 a.m. I remember clearly that you -- they were [indiscernible] by Meho Palo, Satara, Ibro who were policemen. They found them and beat them. They took out Alija Kardas, we just heard a scream and he never got back. Then on the morning of the 23rd of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I just want to know where the 280 of you were put up.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: In two rooms on the floor in the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 77 of your amalgamated statement, you said that you were put up in one room.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You are going too fast ahead. On the 23rd, in the morning, when they beat us up, they forced us to run to a completely different part of the barracks to one room. They continued calling up people's names of people from Hadzici, and it happened on the 20th of June 1992. Priest Milan Lucic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please wait a second. We are still in the barracks. 280 of you were in one room. Now you say two rooms. How big was this room?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: When we arrived on the 23rd of June, but you know very well how big the barracks is. Don't pretend to be naive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this room, how many of you were there? You said in two rooms.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Yes. 280. Then the 47 were later taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How was big -- how big was the room that you were put up in?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, could you repeat your last answer? The interpreters couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, on the 23rd of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The room, the room, sir. How big was the room where you were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: It was 8 by 5 or 6, but I didn't have an opportunity to measure it. We were just pushed in as if we were cattle. I didn't have a measuring stick with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you sitting, were you lying down, what did you do in that room?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: We packed ourselves in half of that room because we didn't know what was going on until Vojo Vukotic came, who worked for the railway company, I used to see him in Blazuj when I was working there as well. He had a list with people's names encircled in red who were supposed to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraphs 81 and 82 of your amalgamated statement, you recalled something only on the occasion of the trial against President Milosevic and your evidence given in those proceedings. You said that you had been maltreated by people wearing Red Berets and some sort of caps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
