utterances.text: Yes, in other words, I was talking about the Special Police forces from Serbia wearing red berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "The policemen in the hall who beat me were all wearing a red berets."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "They spoke in Ekavian." [Interpretation] Ekavian accent. [In English] "They all wore camouflage uniforms, red berets." [Interpretation] And you say: [In English] "I'm sure they were from Serbia, from the city of Nis, in particular. They were members of the Special Forces from Nis, the Nis specialists." [Interpretation] This is how you described them and that prompted and triggered your memory only after you were summoned to testify in the Milosevic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But why did you remember that only in the Milosevic trial? Why you never mentioned that before?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 65 ter 8978, 65 ter 8978, page 5 in Serbian and 7 in English. You say here, the fifth line from the top in the Serbian: "They ordered me to go through the corridor," and between the first and the second, third, well, let's see where the English begins: [In English] "I had to run the gauntlet." [Interpretation] And now you say: They ordered me to go down that hallway and when I started to run down the hallway I had to run the gauntlet made by the military police members wearing red berets, actually those were not red berets but red caps with a yellow sign." Is that what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They were Red Berets, they were the specials from Nis, and when I was at Tomo Kovac's, you skipped, or, you omitted to say that I was there for 48 days. I didn't have any fresh air. I was kept in the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you state what we see in front of us in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you say at the time that you said it was the Red Berets? Why didn't you repeat in the amalgamated statements anything about the red signs on their caps and why didn't you say 1996 that these were specials from Nis?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I could ask you the same thing if you had been treated inhumanely and hiding like a mouse. I would ask you the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let us see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's not appropriate for Mr. Karadzic to ask the witness why something wasn't included in the amalgamated statement. As he well knows, these amalgamated statements are prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor. It would be equivalent to asking a witness why were you not asked a certain question in direct examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat our assertion that the fault of amalgamated statements is the fact that they are the product of the Prosecution, not the product of what the witness said. I'm just asking the witness whether he -- why he added something and why he did not stick to the statement from 1995. But all right, very well, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what else you remembered or what else was suggested to you. Let's look at 1D3362. 1D3362, paragraph 3. Paragraph 3, they are interpreting you here as well: [In English] "In paragraph 84, Mr. Music recalls that at Lukavica he was brought into a room where there were three officers. He stated that they swore on my "balija" mother and one of them kicked me," [Interpretation] and so on and so forth. [In English] "Mr. Music said he believes that the officer who kicked him was Tomislav Sipcic, the Romanija Corps commander. He believes this because when he was previously in The Hague for the Krajisnik case he listened to several intercepted conversations." [Interpretation] You're stating here, thus, that General Sipcic personally beat you, and even though you provided 15 statements and amended statements and mentioned over 150 names, you never mentioned General Sipcic. Who suggested to you to remember that before this particular testimony here in my case?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he must have committed major crimes. If I'm not mistaken, he was a colonel at the time. And as for what you say, all of the things that happened, I have information about because I'm in touch with some of the Serbs of yours from whom I'm receiving information about graves. They said that Momo Mandic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait, wait. Just before testifying in my case, you happened to recall General Sipcic and accused him, accused General Sipcic of beating you, and now you're saying that General Sipcic committed crimes. Is that something that someone suggested to you or you just happened to suddenly recall that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Nobody prepares me, not even my family knows where I am right now. We do not have a tendency to lie just as many Serbs, in quotation marks, do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will take another brief break for 15 minutes. We will resume at half past 11.00. --- Break taken at 11.15 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have about 40 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Excellency, this is the favourite witness of all the OTP witnesses. He's given 15 statements and now we are on paragraph 80 of the amalgamated statement. Really, we need more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can't deal with every aspect. Concentrate on important issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I think that the questions that I did not manage to cover will not be used as a ground for any decisions by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Music, nobody suggested anything to you, thus, but you, yourself, remembered to involve General Sipcic in this particular testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, correct, so somebody suggested him to you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it's correct that nobody suggested it to you, you remembered it yourself?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: My word of honour. Nobody did it, in Bosnia now we have the chequer-board -- I mean this is how all of our politicians are behaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Just to correct the record. Mr. Karadzic says it was the witness who suggested that he involved General Sipcic in this particular testimony. Prior to Mr. Karadzic raising it, it wasn't part of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then perhaps it was the interpretation. I said, Did he recall it himself or did somebody suggest it to him? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Music, let us now briefly look at one P exhibit, P1001, so that we can see how General Sipcic reacts quite strongly to first unconfirmed rumours in relation to a brigade commander. P1001. Yes, this is something else but this is also a document, there is also the front page, all right, just one moment, page 1, ah, there it is, at the top. Kusic, I strictly forbid to you take any action on your own unless I personally approve. Particularly any form of mopping up of anybody's villages. For the last time I'm warning you to refrain from massacres, rampaging, abusing the innocent population of any nationality. Commander Colonel Tomislav Sipcic on 26th of June, 1992. On the 23rd, you had already arrived there and you assert that that colonel, he was a colonel at the time, personally mistreated you and slapped you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fortunately, a protected witness here, we are not going to mention his name, confirmed that these were rumours, and slander, even though he warned Sipcic, even Kusic without any reason?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: We spent three nights there where we were beaten, mistreated, there is nothing that we didn't have to do. We had to cross ourselves, sing different songs. We had to curse Alija. People were hitting us with rifles as we were lying on our stomachs. I don't really want to remember this any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. My question is: After were you in Lukavica, you were transferred to Kula; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were two rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also in two rooms in Kula?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in your statement, you said that you were assigned to rooms.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you need to proceed in order, otherwise you're going to make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you mistreated in Kula?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: In Kula, there were -- this was before we went out on work assignment. We went to Grbavica, we were looting for the Serbs. We went all the way to our lines, front lines. Our people looked at us. They didn't want to fire at us. Everything that was of value was loaded on to trucks and was trucked into the Slavisa Vajner Cica Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was not the question. The question is: Were you mistreated in Kula?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I was questioned, but I was not mistreated in Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that you testify so frequently because some people will not testify, your Muslims from your village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Probably they don't want to see you because you're not really that sympathetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, sir, they don't want to witness in other cases and they are even angry at you because you're testifying; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I don't see any people who are angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 9153. Serbian page 4, English page 5, 65 ter 9153. This is your statement from 2002. In the Serbian, it is one paragraph-but-last: "I could talk about this" and in English, it's -- begins with the words, "Also Nermin Simsic," the last paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say: "Also Nermin Simsic could say more about this as he was together with me in Kula in the same room. And as he was friends with Slobodan Avlijas, who came and brought him cigarettes." Is that Slobodan Avlijas that you accused of mistreating people?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, Slobodan Avlijas is an extremist, I knew him before. He was born in Rakovica and he lived in Hadzici on the same floor as my father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. However, Simsic doesn't want to say anything because he stopped talking with me only because I said that he could testify about this event. So this Nermin Simsic, is he a Muslim from your part of the world?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Not "Simsic" but "Semsic." He was taken out. If he saved his life and prevented him from getting killed, why would he then speak ill of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You said this in 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 91 of your amalgamated statement, you say that you were questioned by Predrag Ceranic in Kula; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he was professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The fact that he was professional and fair to you, this operative of the State Security Service, Predrag Ceranic, why is that not mentioned in paragraph 97 of your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, don't ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we have to take your amalgamated statement with a degree of reserve because it does not quite reflect what you said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain? I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please move on. You raised this and you had heard the explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in the case against it Momcilo Krajisnik, you suddenly recalled Momcilo Mandic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Look, I knew Momcilo Mandic before the war. I knew he was in the police. I saw him on a daily basis because my rooms were some 60 metres away from the entrance that he used every day to go to the canteen where the food was. Some people went with him. I don't know if they were his escorts or not. I was not permitted to come close to the window. I was one metre away from the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. As you see, we don't have too much time. So in all statements to date, before your testimony in the Krajisnik case, you did not mention Mandic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You had the opportunity here to see intercepted conversations provided to you. Everything is there. The then Colonel Tomislav Sipcic, when he spoke, I didn't have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Thank you. So you learned a lot from the material from the intercepted talks; is that corrected?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have as much time as you have to make up certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what post Mr. Momcilo Mandic occupied during the war?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: He was your minister of police, because after that, I was transferred to Ilidza to Tomo Kovac, whom you withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say that because of that he wore a uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they were not wearing the SMB uniforms. Their uniforms were more beige, Avlijas and my neighbour, Milenko Bjelica, as I explained, when they were taking me to Kula, he pretended not to see me and he turned away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We are on Mandic now. Mandic was the minister of justice not the minister of police, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: It's all the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Never in your life you saw Momcilo Mandic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You can't say that. I knew him from seeing him around every day but I didn't know him that he -- I didn't know that he could become just the same kind of extremist person as you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's see what Judge Orie went through in order to establish the truth in your words. You went back and forth with him quite a lot. Look at page 20 of the amalgamated statement where Judge Orie says, and you say -- and you didn't see him on that occasion either, but during Judge Orie's questioning you started to make up arguments in order to get Momcilo Mandic involved in the proceedings against Momcilo Krajisnik. Yes or no; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I have the impression that you're trying to provoke me, but you will not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct what I have just said?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you then lie to Judge Orie?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't lie. I grew up in a family that was such that I'm not used to lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 22 of your amalgamated statement, Judge Orie is speaking to you: [In English] "Let me bring you back again, I'm not asking you what you know about Mr. Mandic and whether he is rich or poor. I am asking you on the base of what you recognised -- you recognised him at the first occasion when he went to the canteen. [Interpretation] Your answer: [In English] "My colleagues said Mandic is coming." [Interpretation] So on and so forth: [In English] "I didn't. I did not move around. I had long hair and a beard, and not even my friends could recognise me when I took -- when they took me out of -- to have my hair cut. [Interpretation] So first of all you saw him, and then you heard from someone that he was coming and then others recognised him instead of you. And you never met him, and you remembered all of that 12 years after the actual occurrences. You never mentioned him in any one of the statements you gave over the past 12 years; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't know his brother and they told me that's his brother who walked in. I knew him well. So that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were not close to the window through which you allegedly saw Mandic; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I had to be about a metre away. A soldier would come and beat us if we would get any closer. There was a dog in front of that window. They called him Alija. You see how much respect they had for our president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 23 and 24 we see that Judge Orie is trying to discern what it is that you're trying to say in order to reach a conclusion. Look at page 25 of your amalgamated statement. How you are concluding something on the basis of pure fabrication: [In English] "Was he accompanied by others when he was -- by other person or by other persons when he was not accompanied by his brother?" [No interpretaiton]. [In English] "Well, they would come in, more of them. I didn't look to see who, what, they were all the same to me, they were all my enemies. [Interpretation] Is this your answer to Judge Orie? Is that right? And then also at the Krajisnik case -- trial, 12 years later, and after 12 statements and addendums, you, all of a sudden, remember that you saw him when you were transferred to the prison in Ilidza; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I saw him in Ilidza. As I described very extensively, I had, I don't know, 15 or 20, oh, come on, I mean, you know when you go upstairs in Ilidza, you know, there were 8 or 2 of us in a room -- there were 8 of us in a room that was 2 by 1 and a half metres, we could barely stand there, let alone lie down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also remember that you saw Krajisnik, and you remember that 12 years after the actual occurrence and it was in relation to your testimony in the Krajisnik case. And you first mentioned this on the occasion of that testimony; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember if it was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at paragraph 110 of your amalgamated statement. The name of Momcilo Krajisnik is mentioned there so we'll find it: [In English] "But I went bak to myself and after some short time, I saw Krajisnik Momcilo through his vent." [Interpretation] Was Mr. Krajisnik also wearing camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 28 of your amalgamated statement, you say that you saw Mr. Krajisnik through the window; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: It's not a window. It's an opening. It's like a cupboard. He was about two or three metres away like these gentlemen sitting here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what you say to Judge Orie: [In English] "I saw a car arriving, but I stood apart because I saw an escort. I knew that somebody was coming. So I stood by the window." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you said that in actual fact you saw him when you were being taken back to the cell; right? That is page 28 of your amalgamated statement. Let me read it out to you: [In English] "Yes, I did straight afterwards. They brought me in and I was coming in through the opposite door. Not the main entrances -- entrance, not the main door, because we were on opposite side and I recognised the man." [Interpretation] So this seems to be different from what you said in relation to that window?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Music, yes, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: It might be helpful to have the full answer that the witness gave which we can see in the statement, but Mr. Music doesn't have it in his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read out the remainder?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic read: "Because we were on opposite side, and I recognised the man, I recognised him when he was coming back, when he was returning."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you still remember the question, Mr. Music?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, since at the time I was cleaning the compound, washing cars, and at one moment the man who was guarding us said, Back inside, somebody is coming. So perhaps I wouldn't have seen him if it wasn't that way, but they didn't really want us to see anything that was going on there. Poplasen also came there. I personally washed his car. The man must have been there for about half an hour. That was the first time I was terrified. He had this enormous knife. He was drunk. He had enormous eyes as well. He had a kokarde, a Serbian kokarde. I'm not going to lie and say that he beat me or something. When he finished washing his car he gave me a pack of cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you saw him from the cell because the door was ajar; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No the door was not ajar. It is a padded door and you cannot really see that. I told you that the door was open looking like a very small book. And when he said, Back inside, somebody is coming, then I paid attention to it. Had he not said that, I wouldn't have paid any attention, I saw Tintor, Poplasen. I saw all of these policemen. You cannot persuade me that it was any different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is not a question of persuasion. Page 28 of your consolidated statement, let us see what Judge Orie is trying to do. And I find that extremely comforting because he didn't succeed either. This is what you said to him: [In English] "I was in the cell. They had taken me back to the cell to prevent me from seeing too much, but I just happened to see it because the door was slightly ajar." [Interpretation] So in this terrible prison, the door is padded and ajar; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You're full of lies. I'm telling you, you are confusing apples and pears, please, it's not that kind of opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what you said. You said a moment ago that the door was padded and that there was an opening there.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: In the middle. And it was at the height of my chin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you're standing up?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what you say on page 29 of the padded statement -- oh, I meant amalgamated statement. This is what Judge Orie says: [In English] "I understand that you saw him through the window in the door or through an opening, the door not being fully closed. Through the opening" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, let's be sure that the witness is following. Do you understand what this is about? The document you're seeing in front of you? That's part of your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, listen, I could know if it were in my own language. And this way it's not really useful for me to be following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is part of your amalgamated statement which you confirmed during the course of your direct examination led by Mr. Hayden. This part refers to your -- all your evidence in the Krajisnik case, and this is part of a conversation you had with Judge Orie at the time. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your answer: [In English] "The door was closed but through the opening, they would always lock the door." [Interpretation] At the end, you say that you saw him as you were sitting, although the little window on the door was as high as your chin; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: As you know full well, you know that because you also came to Tomo Kovac, and it's about half a metre up. And we sat there in order to have some fresh air because there were eight of us and I couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Page 30, this is your answer: [In English] "I was sitting like this, as I am now, and he passed in front of me just a metre away." [Interpretation] And so on. This is what Judge Orie said: [In English] "At what height, approximately, was the opening in the door?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Well, the opening was at the level of my head. "Judge Orie: What would be -- that would be approximately in the middle of the door, taking into account the average height of the door." [Interpretation] This is what you say: [In English] "No, more higher." [Interpretation] Then you go on to describe this. So through this high opening on the door of the cell, as you were sitting, you saw Mr. Krajisnik, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you describe your stay at the Ilidza station, and in paragraph 112, you say that you did not trust Mr. Glavas, who was commander of the station in Ilidza; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he saved the life of one of your family members. He used all his connections in order to enable a wounded man to get to a Muslim hospital, though he had been in three Serb hospitals. Did you describe that, how he made it possible for that ambulance to get through with that wounded man of yours?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: That is true. But it's not -- I cannot lie. But it's not my family. It is a member of my son-in-law's family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now have a look at 1D3360. It is a statement from 2007. In Serbian, page 3; in English, page 5. Zumreta Music, the last paragraph, and then it says: "My third daughter had already been married and she lived in Edvana [phoen] Hercegovacka," that's probably the name of the street, "in Kovacevici." In English, it's around line 10 or 12. You will see the name of Zumreta Music. You say the village was attacked on the 7th of May when my son-in-law's brother was wounded. He was transferred, Serbs also helped - Tihomir Glavas, police commander - to transfer him to Sarajevo because he was seriously wounded but the clerk -- but check-points had already been established and he intervened that he be allowed to pass through the check-points in order to be taken to Sarajevo, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I stand by every word I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 101 of your amalgamated statement, before they transferred you to Ilidza on the 23rd of July 1992, although now in your consolidated statement you changed the date to the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: It is exactly the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at this? Paragraph 102 of the consolidated statement. [In English] "Before we would have gone to work on 21st of July, 1992. On 21st of July 1992, they called out the names of me and five men. We were taken to bus, to a bus, there were women and children there on the bus. We thought we were going to be exchanged, but that didn't happen." [Interpretation] In all your statements so far, just like in the previous consolidated statement, it was the 23rd of July, whereas here you say it's the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: The 21st of July. On the 20th, I was working in Ozrenska digging trenches, working, and a man with a sniper saw me from our side and what could I do? And I turned to him and I looked at him and I thought, It's better for one of my own men to kill me than somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to Ozrenska, it's not true you were digging trenches, you were doing something else. Is it true that on the morning when you arrived in Lukavica, about 44 or even more elderly persons were allowed to go to the Muslim part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: That happened on the 30th of June, 1992; that is to say, 75 persons who were born in around 1936. For example, my father-in-law was born in 1926, he was in that other war. I mean what kind of a soldier was he? They just wanted to loot his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Persons born from 1936 onwards, so people were around 53 or 54, and all of them were released; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: It is the way I said it and I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to the 21st of July. Is -- or, rather, was that a Serb bus, the one that you took?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, it's probably not a Muslim bus. Oh, no, no, no. It was an UNPROFOR bus. UNPROFOR was escorting, that's the first time I saw women and children. As far as I know through Lukavica and Kula, there were 3.000 Bosniaks who went through. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 22205, 65 ter; 65 ter 22205, page 4 in the Serbian and in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's in the middle where you say, "I stayed in Kula until 23rd of July, 1992." And then in the lower part, the other -- the second paragraph which begins, "I remained at Kula until 23rd." I'm going to read in Serbian: "I remained in Kula until 23rd of July 1992, when Asim, Musanovic; Semsic, Nermin; Meho Babic, Jusuf Fejzovic, and Ekrem Nuhanovic and I were called out and told that we were going to be exchanged. After that, an UNPROFOR vehicle came to pick us up. When we arrived in Ilidza we were stopped by the Chetniks at the traffic lights near the old railway station and were told that all of those who were not going to be called out should get out of the vehicle. Accordingly, Raif Fejzovic and I got out of the vehicle and were subsequently taken to the building of the Ilidza SJB where we were detained." So nowhere do you mention women, children or buses. UNPROFOR didn't have any buses. They only had armoured vehicle vehicles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Look, you are so full of lies. Whatever I said I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in this statement you never mentioned women and children or a bus?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Why would I have to mention it? I was taken to Ilidza. I don't know where this exchange took place. Your criminals and our criminals got together and they made some exchange, but you know very well what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While you were in Ilidza SJB, you were being treated fairly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, while you were in village Ilidza, a shell fell near the station, and destroyed a large number of cars, and that, among other things, contributed to your being late for the exchange, or, rather, failing to be exchanged; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because you were afraid nobody went out. They only sent us out to clear up the rubble. So presumably if one shell came, one could have expected another one to come, but I don't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But who was firing at the Serbs at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: There is no name written on a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After that, after this failed exchange, you were returned to the sports centre in Hadzici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: There were 52 detainees from Kula and two from Ilidza, including women and children and elderly, as I said, there was an invalid without both legs, there were children there as well. There were elderly people whom I had to help get to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Were these people willing to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No. It was ordered for them to do that, to collect all their belongings, they gave them only 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that. So in paragraph 117, you say: [In English] "They never reached any agreement regarding the exchange, and at a certain point, all the buses went to Hadzici. They stopped in front of the sports hall and we were all unloaded there. There were about 500 of us. I" -- [Interpretation] And a little bit down. [In English] "I was together with my wife and family." [Interpretation] Then again, downwards: [In English] "Then there was my brother and my sister-in-law, my brother's son who was retarded." [Interpretation] When you were taken prisoner in Musici, that was a time when the Serbs left the women and the children as well as your brother because he had a retarded child?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That was done by a friend of his, who used to work with his father but these are extremists, Dragan Prodan, they used to have trailer trucks --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. The 14 of you were captured and taken away, whereas the women and children, including your brother because he had a retarded child, were left alone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you say that on that occasion, or, rather, when you returned from this failed exchange, you were reunited with your brother, her husband -- his wife and the other brother who had this retarded child.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. And including my father who was born in 1924.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now it's time to wrap up your cross-examination. You have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will really do my best to reduce the number of questions as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you testify against Rade Veselinovic despite the fact that you were not an eyewitness of any of his crimes and that was in the Bosnia-Herzegovinian court?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: This person maltreated me more than anyone else. When I left the camp and became a member of the commission, I didn't dare say that I was on the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you testify against him in the Bosnia-Herzegovinian court?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have 1D3361 -- 0, while we are waiting, you said that you -- he had maltreated you and you took your revenge by testifying against him.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: You are full of lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D3360. Page 7 in Serbian and page 11 in English. Last paragraph, you were asked by the Prosecutor as follows: "Were you ever an eyewitness to him having liquidated anyone, abused, beaten, maltreated anyone," and so forth. And you say: "I wasn't. I only recounted my version and what I experienced, and it is undeniable that Rade Veselinovic was a member of the police and that he was moving across the area." He was, therefore, convicted for being a member of the police and he was in the area, but you never saw any act that he committed. Therefore, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I know that he was present when the 12 Bosniaks and two Croats were shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you present there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: This is a stupid question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's now talk about the exchanges. You say that the civilians who were to be exchanged were given half an hour to pick up their belongings?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes, don't lie. I said 15 minutes, five minutes ago. Don't change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you request which particular civilians would be exchanged? Did you ask for your wife and other relatives of yours to be exchanged, and in exchange the Serbs were supposed to release some of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we briefly look at 1D3363. 1D3363. You say, and I'm going to read it, I don't know if there is a translation, it's a statement that you gave, and I quote: "I hereby declare that I'm leaving Vesel Kotodorovic [phoen], father's name, Nedeljko Hadzic [indiscernible] number 33. I leave to him in custody until my return the following items: Gornja TV, washing machine, refrigerator, and other items that are going to left in the safe custody of the above named, and that no compensation was requested in return." So this was done by your wife?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. People used to leave houses and cars and things like that. I know where this man lives and I would like Todorovic, Gavro to be faced with this. That's the son of this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at your statement given on 16th of June, 1997, and then on the 26th of June 1997? But before that, can we have the document which is currently on the screen being tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification, pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1116, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, in -- can we have in e-court your 1997 statement? 65 ter 9091. If we had time, it's a very instructive statement, and valuable, so if I'm granted some additional time by you are Excellencies, I will get back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to conclude. How long do you expect for your re-examination, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Conclude by 25 past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 14, that is the penultimate page in English and I believe it's the same page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm only going to repeat what you said and I would just like you to confirm whether it's correct or not. Who suggested to you to call certain people "weekend Chetniks?"

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: A friend of mine from the Ilidza police told me that and I didn't know before that. I used to see various people in various uniforms who would come over on Friday and leave on a Monday. I'm not going to tell you his name because he told me not to walk around Ilidza too much because I would get killed. They used to kill Croats en masse. I don't know what they were actually doing, but I have to say that they treated me in an extremely fair and correct manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The manager of the Hadzici sports centre also treated you in a correct way?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay, at Ilidza, but how about Lukavica and Kula, did they treat you fairly as well?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because that was Mr. Kovac. Glavas was playing a double game. He saved some people but he also shot dead some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said on this page that you were never taken to perform forced labour in Svrake.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They did but they spared me because I was too exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you mentioned human shield. Is it used if an army is advancing or retreating?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please slowly repeat his answer from the very beginning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Music, interpreters missed your beginning part of your answer. Could you repeat from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, from what I know, it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. Do you think that human shield is being used when an army is advancing or retreating and then they place civilians between them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: When they were advancing, because they were cowards, they only felt brave when they were firing from artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Music, so you're saying that the Serbian army was advancing and using you as a human shield. Where was it advancing?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: They couldn't have advanced anywhere where there was Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let's go back. What you said in this penultimate part, and it says here that both sides asked that their civilians be released and Kobiljaca is mentioned here. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it says that both sides asked for their civilians to be set free. That's what you stated?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at the last page, and I can read it. You said to a Serb, or, rather, you made an arrangement with a Serb and you say: "For the third time when I came there, there was a man who asked for six men from our side, three women and three children. I asked for my wife, my father, my brother, his wife and their two children. That's the arrangement that I made to meet this Serb within seven days. I told him that he should allow my family to take their belongings with them, and I guaranteed him that his family would be allowed the same. After we agreed on this, we both went to the police on our respective sides, in order to prepare the papers. That depended on whether people wanted to be exchanged. After we received the decision to proceed with the exchange, and after the exchange was completed, we had to go back to the police with the papers confirming from the other side in each case to the effect that the exchange was carried out and that the civilians were safe." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I took it by force and the Serbs were involved in that because they used to change --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. How many times did your wife attempt to be exchanged and the rest of your family?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, she was supposed to be exchanged on the 7th as promised, but since the exchange failed, as I described in my previous statement when the shell fell, on the 8th, that was just a deception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Now my last topic, Mr. Music. Had you seen me in Hadzici before and during the war?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Several times before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And during the war?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? I was in the camp during the war. I couldn't have seen you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you mention that earlier in your statement, that you had seen me at least 15 times that I had my car painted, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I said that in February. You cannot deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Why didn't you mention that before?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't feel the need. I hoped that you would drop dead, but I must say that I'm very happy to see you here and I think you will end up as your mentor, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So today you said that for the first time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that I was never in Hadzici, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: That you are lying. We had people who were following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, who followed me, some sort of secret service of yours?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, these people from the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. And they followed me before the war as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did you establish the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Don't ask me that. I wasn't there. I'm not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was that legal for you to follow me?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: In the same way that it's not legal for you to rape, loot, rob. Why didn't you ask me how many people were in Hadzici? 26.6 per cent of the inhabitants were Serbs, but you were at all the positions in the authority, you didn't want to divide power with Croats and Muslims and that is why you began the war. The war began in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's round off this topic: Was I followed by your Crisis Staff or the Patriotic League, did you have a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, Mr. Music, I wish you all the best, a safe return home, and now I see exactly why you are a favourite witness. Wherever the OTP appears, Mr. Music appears as well.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Well, look, you are not favourite among my people or anyone else because you are the greatest aggressor after Hitler. You walked around Sarajevo. I remember well in 1991 what you said in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am still hearing those words ring.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Say what that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I never used this switch to turn microphones off, but next time you're making unnecessary statements, I may use it, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I note that was the third time today Mr. Karadzic has described this witness as a favourite of the Prosecution. It's a phrase that he's used before. He's been told it's inappropriate and he continues to use it. I note that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Music, I just have a few extra questions for you. Just before, and I'm looking at transcript page 68, you were asked by Mr. Karadzic, okay, at -- you -- he was asking you about your treatment and whether you were treated fairly. And he asked you about Lukavica and Kula, and you said, yes, you were treated fairly because that was Mr. Kovac. I just wanted to clarify whether your response referred to both Kula and Lukavica or just one of those places.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Just for the Ilidza MUP, where Tomo Kovac was the chief of the police until the accused appointed him as a minister in Pale, police minister. He was replaced by Tiho Glavas, then who came, I think, on the 6th of August, I think, in 1992. In Lukavica, I went through hell there and I don't like to remember that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Earlier today, Mr. Music, and I'm looking at transcript page 44, Mr. Karadzic took you to paragraphs 81 and 82 of your statement, and he asked you or he said to you, "in those paragraphs you recalled something only on the occasion of the trial against President Milosevic and your evidence given in those proceedings. You said that you had been maltreated by people wearing red berets and some sort of caps. Is that correct?" If I can have 65 ter 09091, please. If we can go to page 9 of both versions. In the middle of the page, Mr. Music, it states here, and I believe you can read the B/C/S version also in the middle of the page: "The policemen in the hall who beat me were all wearing red berets. From the way they spoke and swore, I could tell that they were not from here." If we can go to page 1 of both versions. Can you confirm, Mr. Music, this is a statement you gave in 1997?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And you testified in the Slobodan Milosevic proceedings in 2002; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Just for the record, the portion I have noted was footnoted in the amalgamated statement that was provided to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Music, Mr. Karadzic today raised a piece of information you recently provided about Mr. Tomislav Sipcic. I just wanted to further clarify that piece of information. You say in your statement that you were kicked by a man you believed to be an officer and that you did not know the identity of that man. Is it the case that before testifying in the Krajisnik proceedings, you did not know the identity of that man?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And what was it that occurred in The Hague when you came to testify in the Krajisnik proceedings that led you to believe that that man may have been Tomislav Sipcic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Listening to the intercept, and I don't know who furnished it, in the evening on the 20th or the 21st of October, when we were supposed to be transferred to Semizovac, Svrake, from the sports hall, the intercepted conversation that I listened to about that, Krajisnik was issuing orders to Mandic, and Mandic to Slobodan Avlijas, that they should transfer us to Svrake because our lines were moving, and so we were needed to be in Hadzici -- we were needed into Hadzici to serve as human shields because 11 people from Hadzici were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, so it was from listening to an intercept that was provided to you when you were in The Hague; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And since the Krajisnik proceedings in 2004, have you testified or given any evidence to the ICTY until today?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: I gave statements to our institutions, the SIP, for example, sometimes when they bring these people in, then they would question me, what they did, how they did it, then we have information from some Serbs who are not extremists about what was done, how it was done, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. But none of those institutions were the ICTY; is that right, Mr. Music?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That concludes the redirect examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I do have one matter to put on the record while we've got an opportunity, this relates to a previous witness. Just to note for the record, that there is a public version now available for Witness KDZ304, under 65 ter 90211A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Music. That concludes your evidence. Thank you on behalf of the Tribunal and this Bench for coming to The Hague yet again to give it. And now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. It's my pleasure to experience an extremist here that Europe will not see the likes of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Witness, that's an entirely unnecessary and unhelpful comment. I reiterate the thanks for you coming to the Tribunal. This is not an opportunity to vent personal views but simply to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for half an hour, and I take it the next witness should be ready. We will resume at five past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to raise one preliminary matter that the Court might already have anticipated and that I discussed with Mr. Robinson earlier. That is the fact that the Prosecution may be using information that falls within the category of impeaching the witness. The Court may be aware of that by virtue of the fact that the previous testimony which gave rise to the 92 ter reflects, indeed, efforts by the Prosecution to illuminate certain issues that were raised. Indeed I think the approach taken in the Krajisnik case was cited in the Popovic judgement or decision as one of the alternative ways of approaching these matters in furtherance of the pursuit of truth. I would be inclined, I might add, to utilise the same kind of procedure which does not involve moving to leading questions immediately but trying to elicit from the witness initially his position and then moving progressively through any previous information provided or documentation before any kind of direct confrontation was -- took place. As I say, I don't think this is the kind of situation that gives rise to much ambiguity in terms of the use of previous information provided or other documentation, and I think falls squarely within the jurisprudence but I wanted to raise it early so we had a minimal amount of disruption to the proceedings as we went through, if and when such instances occurred. And, of course, I would also distinguish that as I know the Court will, and as the previous decisions has, from -- have from instances where it's simply refreshing recollection or clarifying ambiguities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have some guidance from the Appeals Chamber's jurisprudence. Do you have any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's better to wait and see how it develops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's bring in the witness. While we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, may I refer to the accused's motion, second motion, for admission of supplemental statement of Rule 92 bis witness, Andja Gotovac, to which the Prosecution didn't oppose the request. Given that the statement has now been duly certified by a presiding officer of the Registrar, then we'll grant it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, it was signed by the witness but has not yet been duly certified by the presiding officer. So we were asking you to grant the admission of the supplemental statement subject to its certification by the presiding officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, that will be done. And a Rule 90(E) warning necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was given in -- previously, Your Honour, and I'm not aware of any particular change of circumstances, so if the Court is guided by the approach in the previous case, that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. Mr. Prstojevic, are you hearing what I'm saying to you now in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did hear it, and I understand, but I probably will not have to use that. I won't be needing to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you are aware of it and have been explained by the Victim and Witness Section but I have to continue. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question. However, in such a case, we will make it sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. I take it you understand what I have just told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prstojevic. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we begin just by having you state your full name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am Nedjeljko Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Prstojevic, is it correct that you testified before this Tribunal in the trial of Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik in June of 2005, specifically from June 14th to June 20th of 2005?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Prstojevic, have you had an opportunity to review that previous testimony through the use of the audiotapes of the testimony that took place?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did have the opportunity to look at the audiotapes of my testimony a few days ago, since the time that I've been here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Prstojevic, is it correct that the answers -- if you were asked the same questions in this proceeding, that your -- the information you would provide would be substantially the same to those questions, and that your position is that the information you provided is accurate?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Basically, I stand by the truth. I'm not going to deny anywhere what I have said, but I do have a series of remarks regarding what happened in the trial of Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, from additions to my CV, to reminding everyone of my statement given to The Hague investigators dated the 26th of March, 2009, and on what I said to you a few days ago, since I've been here, that regarding all the issues, I can provide certain detail, certain statistical data, that there are a lot of leading questions there, and imposed ones, and that there are certain sections where even the Trial Chamber said to me that they don't understand me when I respond to certain questions or that I saw that the Trial Chamber -- that judge didn't understand that it was a wartime situation, but talked about barricades. So in order to be able to look at the entirety of my statement, and to be able to understand over 208 intercepted conversations of mine here and some other documents, I would like to augment my statement to remind everyone of the statement that I gave to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal and to have explained to me, even when I was giving the statement to the investigators, I thought that that related only to me and not that it would be used in the trials of other persons, because I am not really up to that and I wouldn't do it unless I have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's break that down, Mr. Prstojevic, to see how we can best proceed. First of all, you understand that the statements given to interviewers previously do not comprise part of your 92 ter statement and are not the subject of the information that will be provided in written form to the Court at this time, although you are free to refer to those interviews in answering any questions put to you by myself or by the accused or by the Court? You understand that? In other words, only your testimony in the Krajisnik case is being tendered at this point which I understood you to say you stand by.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but, please, I voiced certain kind requests here. I can immediately say that I can only accept the cross-examination in its entirety by the lawyers and by Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, in its entirety. Other parts, I can accept but I do have seven points in respect of that. Actually, not seven, ten, where I need to augment certain things, certain points I would need to add one name; for example, I said four persons were present, but now I know that there was a fifth person also present about whom I know that was very important. So I will be adding a name in one point. In another point I will be adding two or three arguments, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Prstojevic, let's -- if you then are seeking to clarify or correct portions of the testimony that will be submitted as -- or that is proposed for submission as 92 ter, can you proceed to do so now? But I would ask you to be as succinct, concise and efficient as possible under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: So I would like to understand correctly if I will be allowed to add some information to my CV because there is some imprecisions during the previous trials as to what I was doing on the basis of volunteering and what was it that I did as a professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, that's not uncommon. However, this shouldn't be an opportunity to augment the pre-existing record with information that might not have been solicited previously because it's not so relevant to the proceedings. So if you'll proceed and if you'll permit me to indicate to you or have the Judges indicate to you that perhaps that's more information than is appropriate under the circumstances, or necessary under the circumstances, then you can proceed, with the Court's permission, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take it that you have a proofing time with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only proofing that took place with this witness was to allow him to listen to approximately 25 to 28 intercepts and also a couple of videos so that if they were raised in court, it would be -- it would reduce the amount of time necessary so they wouldn't have to be played in their entirety again. But beyond that, under these circumstances, there was no conventional proofing in the manner the Court is inquiring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you are aware of those parts in relation to which the witness wishes to augment or change his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no more information than the Court has at this point. We provided -- essentially when Mr. Prstojevic arrived, and he can confirm this, I indicated to him what the Court schedule would be, advised him of the process involving 92 ter, he essentially confirmed his Krajisnik testimony, but indicated he would like to listen to it again, and then also listen to the intercepted telephone conversations over the course of the next -- of the following days, and the audiotapes of the Krajisnik testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber will hear how you can manage with the witness in terms of augmentation or revision of his previous document. I'm just asking, maybe thinking aloud, how burdensome it will be if you are ordered to lead his evidence live, viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the burden versus the efficiency is impossible to know at this point. Perhaps we can find out from -- as I say, my understanding from two previous contacts with Mr. Prstojevic was that he stood by the Krajisnik testimony, and so there was no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In relation to the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no in the entirety of the testimony as I understood it from both contact through the OTP in 2009, which is -- and also the most recent contact. It may well be that the corrections or augmentation that Mr. Prstojevic has in mind are of such a nature, and that's what I would have anticipated given the information he provided us before, that they will take approximately -- hopefully ten minutes or so. In that case, I think it's more efficient to move forward with the 92 ter process. Otherwise, if we are looking at a lengthy process, then the Court may be correct that we are better advised approaching this in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll see how the witness confirms the veracity of his previous testimony. And we'll deal with it when we have seen his evidence in relation to that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Prstojevic, if we can proceed, again I would ask you to be as succinct and concise as possible in making whatever corrections you have to make. And with respect to your CV, again, if there is something of significance that you think really merits clarification, that's fine, but I don't think the record has to be augmented with your complete biography.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will add. But Mr. Tieger, I apologise to you even though I shouldn't have to apologise. On the 22nd -- on the 26th of February, 2011, when we talked together I literally told to you I accept and will not deviate anywhere from what I said in the -- my testimony in the Krajisnik case. But since I am now testifying in regard to a different person, that I came without any preparation or talks, that I have some details that I needed to clarify and add. I have some arguments I need to state and put some questions, and, if necessary, I would need to mention some witnesses. So in order to be as brief as possible I just wanted to mention a few things regarding my CV. What is important to add to my biography is that on the 1st of December 1991, I was a secretary in the inspection service. Then on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to read a little bit more slowly for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I'm sorry to not understand B/C/S so we have to rely on interpreters, so they will be benefited if you speak a bit slower. If -- in particular, when you read out something, please slow down. So could you start again after you were a secretary in the inspection service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 28th of June, 1991, I became the head of the municipal board of the Ilidza SDS as a volunteer. On the 5th of April, 1992, I was the president of the municipality of Ilidza until the end of the war. I would like to add that before the war, I was a reserve officer, sergeant class 1, and I received a lot of awards and received recognition for a number of training exercises, as a leader of an artillery company and so on and so forth. I was promoted captain on the 28th of June 1993. What is important, though, is this: I want to say that throughout the whole war, I was a member of the Ilidza Brigade as a soldier, regardless of rank, and that in critical points in time I would lock the municipal building, I would release the administration service, and I would take up a rifle and fight as a regular soldier, as an infantryman. I often would place the still-smoking gun, lean it against the wall and pick up the telephone in order to complete some other administrative business. This would be what I wanted to say about my CV. And now I would like to add some things that I had in relation to the Krajisnik testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not overlap with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would just need to intervene that the witness just said that after he said that he leaned his still-smoking rifle, that smelled of gunpowder and had to carry out his work in such a psychological state. Perhaps you can ask the witness if he confirms that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you were going to proceed. Mr. Karadzic's intervention should be a reminder that you'll need to speak at such a pace that the interpreters can keep up.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we move on to these additions in relation to the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: The first addition has to do with 093, that instruction for working in emergencies. In addition to the forementioned persons, in attendance was also the commander of the Territorial Defence, Dragan Markovic. And I saw from the Krajisnik testimony and also with my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, we don't follow what that 93 is. Could you help us, Mr. Tieger? That should refer to an exhibit number in Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, P960, Your Honour. It's now P960 in our case and in the -- I think it's labelled as such in the associated exhibits as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry for interruption. Mr. Prstojevic, could you begin from when you saw from the Krajisnik testimony and please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the Republican Assembly of the Serb people of the Serb Democratic Party that was attended by over 500 persons. That is what I wish to say with regard to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed? Second question: A conversation with Mr. Tomo Kovac, chief of the public security station of Ilidza, and Cedo Kljajic, a high-ranking official of the Centre of Public Security Services in Vraca, the 20th of April, 1992. This is the moment when Cedo Kljajic is reporting to our chief in Ilidza that all the Muslim leaders in the MUP were asked to come to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to an agreement to attack Ilidza. One member of the Trial Chamber asked whether they went out there to reach agreement to tear down the barricades. I wish to explain this. On all roads at that time there were check-points. People were still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Are you in the position to tell us what page it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a reference -- oh, I can do so, Your Honour. First of all, it's at pages 14545 through -46, and 14559 through -61, and I believe that's a reference to 65 ter 30689.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On all roads, there were people coming and going to and from work. As they did. And also trucks with food. However, there were machine-gun nests around them because the armies were facing each other because there was a war going on. We already had casualties. We had people who were dead and wounded by then. Already on the 27th of April, that is to say only within seven days, according to official sources, both Muslim sources and our own, there were about 1.000 dead persons in Sarajevo, both Serbs and Muslims. That means that I want to point out that there was a war going on. The war practically started on the 3rd of April in Ilidza. And I can say something else. I can refer to another document. Already on the 15th of April, Muslim units that were attacking us said that they ran out of ammunition. I have those documents with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prstojevic. Let me only say that, please, rather than make corrections and expand with argumentation, if you can just make the correction as simply and directly as possible, that will expedite the process. If you could move to the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: You have a document that is summons to a Serb soldier who was thinking of his fatherland. I cannot understand, yet again, what the problem is with that document and what kind of a problem you have with that document because that wasn't discussed at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, by way of guidance, and I believe the Court would have offered the same, that is not in the nature of a correction to your testimony but a reaction to, I gather, what you think either the Prosecution, the Defence or the Judges were thinking about it. So if you could focus on the testimony you gave, and any augmentation specifically or correction specifically to that, rather than trying to argue with an unseen interlocutor, that would be much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am not carrying on a discussion with an invisible interlocutor.
