Mr. Tieger, you are accusing me on account of that document, saying that it is proof of something that is contrary to international conventions related to war. So let us see what this is all about. I personally wrote that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, whether or not Mr. Tieger is criticising you, the answer given at the time was a correct one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was correct, but I don't understand at all why I'm being accused and that's what I wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, let's be clear about the process we are engaged in now. I will be attempting -- I will be asking you additional questions, attempting to elicit information from you, which -- to which I will be expecting responses that are focused on the question. The accused will be doing the same for many hours, I might add, so you'll have ample opportunity, I suspect, to delve into whatever issues you may have in mind, and the Court may also ask questions. So whatever you may think the implications of the questions are, that is the purpose, and you're not being accused in this manner, you're being asked questions, and asked to respond to those questions. If I could ask you then to move on to your next correction, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: The next correction is the declaration on the work of the Serb Democratic Party in wartime conditions. The Prosecutor is dealing with our declarative introduction. This involves romantic rhetoric but it is true. It doesn't deal with a single one of our tasks. What it is that we are going to strive for during the war and what we are going to try to carry out, and what I stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Next one is a MUP document of the 20th of September, 1993. I had it in my hands briefly in the courtroom. The Chamber said that they did not understand my answers and my comments in relation to that document. Could I please have insight into this document and may I provide my comments with regard to that document yet again so that the Trial Chamber would understand me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Would you like to make some different observation on that document from what you gave in earlier evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Absolutely not. I have no idea what the document is about, but if I were to read it, then I could explain and then the Trial Chamber would understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow, Mr. Tieger. Could you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is an invitation by the witness to be given an opportunity to review and comment on something further, and I -- it seems to me that either party or the Court is free during the course of his examination and his testimony here to do so, but I don't think it falls within the purview of the current exercise of correcting the statement. As I understand it, the comments given in response during the Krajisnik testimony were accurate. It's something that the witness would like to have an opportunity to do. Anybody can take that on board given the time we have but I think we can move on to the next correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear him out about the points you want to make. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next thing I wish to say is in it relation to the decision of the 2nd of April, 1993. It's a decision of the War Presidency of the Serb Municipality of Ilidza on banning the return of Croats and Muslims. I have some documents here that explain the situation and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, let me ask you if the information you provided in connection with your testimony about that document was accurate or if there is something specific you want to correct about what you said during the Krajisnik case about the decision of the War Presidency on banning the return of Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: The information that I provided is correct. However, now I have some information to the effect that immediately when this decision was being implemented, we received 150 Croat families on the basis of the approval given by the HVO of Kiseljak whereby they were allowed to leave Kiseljak and that was during the month when that decision was valid. I have the document here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And your next point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next correction has to do with the 17th session of the People's Assembly of the Republika Srpska, the date is the 24th of July, 1992. If I knew then what I know now, I would not have commented upon that document at all. I am convinced that the OTP does not have the original document from our Assembly from Pale. Yesterday, I saw the initial part of the document that was typed out on our Cyrillic typewriter, and then somebody started typing on a typewriter that uses the Latin script, and that's not ours. Further on, in that document, the key words, whereby the OTP is proving something or trying to prove something, are translated, believe it or not, in three different ways, one word is translated in three different ways. The Trial Chamber has the word, "protjerali." I, in two documents, have the word, "potisli," and then in another one, "potjerali." And there are other translations there that are incorrect as well. However, why do I insist on this so much? Mr. Tieger gave himself the right to say that it's one and the same word, "protjerali" and "potisli," that these two words mean the same thing in the Serbian language, which is completely incorrect. It is like the sky and the earth. And I think that this part in the Latin script is a forged document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you said about that document, 17th session in Krajisnik trial, was false?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could intervene. This is repetition of what the witness said in the Krajisnik case, essentially with some expansion, and I think the witness will confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, Mr. Tieger, I cannot apologise to you on account of things that I'm right about. When I am not in the courtroom, you claim to the Trial Chamber that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, hold on a second, please. First of all, I'm not quite sure how you know what happened when you weren't in the courtroom but that's not the subject of what we are doing right now. We are talking about your testimony in the Krajisnik case. Now, the question I just asked you was whether or not during the course of the Krajisnik case, you made essentially the same point about your speech at the 17th Assembly session in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did say that but on the CDs I heard the other day, and that's how I know what you were talking about with the Trial Chamber, but at any rate, I heard you convincing the Trial Chamber that it's one and the same word. I was not in the courtroom then. Please listen to the CD. Also, I saw that it wasn't our original document. It is not an authentic document. It is not a court document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. So the information you gave to the Court in response to questions concerning your speech at the 17th Assembly session during the course of the Krajisnik case was accurate and you're reiterating your concerns about that speech; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it means that I did not know those two things then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Next correction, please?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think I have two more corrections. The next correction has to do with the conversation between the minister of justice, Mr. Mandic, and yours truly, on the 2nd of June 1992. I would like it best if this conversation were to be replayed here so that this Honourable Trial Chamber could hear this conversation, because the Prosecutor was so persistent in trying to prove something that was not actually the case, that that is quite astonishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, was your testimony --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- in connection with that conversation during the course of the Krajisnik case accurate? And do you have anything about your testimony or the information you provided about that that you wish to correct? That document, I believe, is in evidence and the Court will have every opportunity to listen to it.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: The statement is correct, but I would like to explain. At the moment of that conversation, Minister Mandic is sitting in Ilidza just like me, except that he is at a position that has a better view and he knows what is happening in Ilidza better than I do. And he cannot say, when I ask him, where I presented an ultimatum, he cannot say that because he doesn't have that kind of information. It's not correct. My second addition, I am surprised and taken aback by this. I am saying that he should go on speaking because I cannot realise what he is on about, but I see that it's being interpreted as if I had confirmed something to him. Thirdly, we are not giving the names of the judges at all. As a matter of fact, that falls under his jurisdiction. The sincerity of my conversation can be seen at the very end when I go on opposing the minister and when I say, "Oh, please, in relation to what the Muslims did to the Serbs of Ilidza, I cannot do that."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And your final correction, please, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: The last one is the most difficult one and I left it to the end. It's an intercepted conversation of the 14th of May, 1992. At that time, this was a person I did not know. When you listen to the conversation several times, you can see who it is. I stand by the conversation here as well but I would like it best if that were to be replayed again, because the Prosecution is trying to prove on the basis of that that we persecuted and deported the Muslim population, which is not correct. This is precisely a conversation when I left my rifle aside, when we had been fighting from 5.08 until twilight. We had eight dead within our ranks, 50 wounded persons, and when I ran in from my visit to the wounded, and it was at twilight, all of this was happening between 12.00 and 14.00 and that is what it was about. So the conversation did not affect at all anything that had happened before 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prstojevic. In fact, I'll be happy to go over that conversation again during the course of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with those corrections, I would tender 65 ter 22235.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think if I was sitting on the Chamber, I would want to hear this witness viva voce. But if you feel that you're -- I think it's really your call, but I think it's difficult to understand the Krajisnik testimony in light of the witness's explanations for it, and it would be better if we all hear what he has to say from scratch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I will hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's quite the contrary. The Court will have -- I'm going to go over various aspects of the events of 1992 and 1992 through 1995. The Court will be deprived of a tremendous amount of courtroom effort and time, and a tremendous amount of information that will illuminate both this witness's testimony and the events. So the contrary is true, and we are going to be hearing approximately, what, 13, 14 hours of testimony from this witness, so there is plenty of viva voce testimony to come. It will be very, very usefully augmented by 22235.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time is time to take a break. We'll break for 15 minutes. And we will come back to that issue when we resume. --- Break taken at 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber, having considered Mr. Robinson's proposal to hear Mr. Prstojevic viva voce, not pursuant to Rule 92 ter as proposed by the Prosecution, agrees that in light of the extent of the corrections made by the witness in court today, his evidence should be led viva voce, as the Chamber is not satisfied that the third prong of Rule 92 ter A is met in this case. Mr. Tieger, we will give you as much time as you need for your direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'm going to -- wouldn't normally do this but I'd like to raise the matter quickly again, either for clarification or for reconsideration, and I'd like to do that outside the presence of the witness, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Prstojevic, there are some matters for us to discuss in your absence, if you could excuse yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a preliminary matter, Your Honour, I raised previously my concerns about both being confronted belatedly with objections from the Defence to which the Prosecution has essentially no time to respond. This is another instance. This matter has been a 92 ter matter for a long, long time, and in particular, what was tendered as 92 ter was testimony under oath in front of this very institution. Now, the Court referred to corrections he made. I agree that the witness spoke for a long time but he didn't resile from a single thing he said. He -- what he did instead was to argue the implications of some of the evidence that was presented, to offer further emphasis on his interpretation as he offered at the time, but he resiled from nothing. The Prosecution fulfilled in full the terms of 92 ter. An objection was raised under -- in -- I must say, a rather half-hearted objection was raised in light of the fact, I would submit, that we had fully complied with the terms of 92 ter, and the result is that we -- the possibility, if this stands, of what I would consider to be an injustice, and that is that we have to go over the same ground that this institution invested a great deal of time in eliciting very carefully, with very lengthy examination and very lengthy cross-examination, and by way of illustration, Your Honour, I mean, it would be possible for me, of course, to simply take this witness through the whole question and answer process of his Krajisnik testimony, and should he deviate from any of those answers then to take him back to that transcript. That process has been completed under oath and the witness has affirmed it in its entirety. I would urge the Court under the circumstances here, that is the circumstances in which this was raised belatedly after the Prosecution had noticed it, in view of the fact that his testimony under oath, in view of the detail and utility of the information, and in light of the fact that the witness did not resile from any of it, this complies fully with 92 ter. I'm happy to invest time in various aspects of eliciting information from the witness, which I intended to do anyway, but it shouldn't gainsay the admission of the -- of 65 ter 22235, which fully complies with the Rules and the practice of this institution and indeed in this very case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to make observations in response to Mr. Tieger's point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I don't think that this is that big of a deal. It's a question of time and it's a question of how you want to hear the evidence, because Mr. Tieger will have the opportunity to lead the witness chronologically through all of these events and it will take a little longer, yes, but I think it will make the evidence more clear. And I think he'd be advantaged by that as well as the Chamber. So I am not sure why it's such a big point of contention. The other thing is that I don't think that the witness has really attested that the written transcript accurately reflects his declaration of what he would say if he was examined. He's put so many caveats on it that I think you're correct in having reservations about whether the Rule itself under 92 ter(A)(3) has been satisfied. But our feeling is basically that we are here to be sure the Chamber hears the evidence in the best way possible so that you make the best possible decision, and, therefore, we would leave it up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we would stand by the ruling we just made. First, it is always the Chamber's discretion whether or not to order the witness to be led viva voce. So I don't see much injustice in there. And second, although the witness confirmed what he said in the trial of Krajisnik, given the corrections, augmentations or additions or supplements, even in relation to those parts he didn't refer to, we are not safely sure whether or not he will be saying the same answers when asked again. So that's the crux of our ruling, and we are not minded to reconsider the ruling we made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Court has made its ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to suggest we could simply ask the witness if -- who has -- who has not only testified under oath but just listened to the entirety of his testimony and offered the elaborations that he did with respect to that entire testimony, if he stands by his testimony with -- in light of the comments he made and if his answers would be the same with the exception of the expansions or argumentation he offered. And that might resolve it. I'm sorry, Your Honour, to do that, but part of the problem was that -- as I pointed out more than once, is that the witness was simply repeating the same argumentation he offered during the course of the Krajisnik case, so it was -- they were not corrections, they were further efforts to make the same point or underscore the same point that he made during the course of his testimony, which is why he stood by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But addition or argumentation is part of changes, corrections, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's a dangerous road to go down. The Rule, as I recall, asks whether or not the witness -- first of all, it's a funny rule when you think about testimony given under oath, which is already a little bit different from a declaration out of court to which the witness attests and says, I'd say the same thing in court. Now you're asking the witness, Would you say the same thing in court you said in court? Be that as it may, in this case, the question nevertheless remains: Does the witness attest that the declaration he gave previously is accurate and he stands by it and would provide the same answers, and I'm -- the fact that he wishes to reargue it or use it as a platform for providing other information he thinks the Court might want to have or might -- he might wish the Court to have, doesn't affect compliance with 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the point, but we've made that ruling for the reasons that it would be safe and clearer to the Chamber in understanding the context of the witness's evidence. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we are bringing in the witness, it's my understanding from speaking with Mr. Tieger that the testimony of this witness is going to be interrupted so that on Tuesday we hear the testimony of another witness. I'll just indicate that's our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We allow the Prosecution to liaise with the witness or via the VWS for the purpose of scheduling matters. And we allow the Defence to have ten hours for its cross-examination, but since the evidence in-chief is to be led live, we may reconsider the amount of time later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, during your absence we decided that your evidence is to be led viva voce so we'll not rely on your prior testimony. So you will give your testimony anew in this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you augmented your CV, but that was an augmentation that was based on the transcript so let me ask you just a couple of questions about your background. You became president of the municipal board of the SDS on June 28, 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Prstojevic, I know you have the habit, I know from the Krajisnik case, you have the habit of writing down questions sometimes, and I see now you're actually referring to a notebook. We would appreciate being advised if you're testifying from your own memory or if you're referring to a document and relying on a document.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to testify on the basis of my memory. However, if the Trial Chamber would allow me, I would use the original documents and some notes of mine. Here is an example: As far as my CV is concerned, I would like to consult my papers because I don't want to make a wrong date. For example, I mentioned medical problem that I had and that I mentioned during the Krajisnik case, and it happened in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, the transcript does not reflect which kind of medical problem was in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That may be because nobody asked him about his medical problem and I'd like to conduct this examination-in-chief without any unnecessary interventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Were you referring to the omission in the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, did you -- what did you say about medical problem? Did you specify your medical problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1996, I had a cold, and when a bridge was being opened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was in answering the previous question by Mr. Tieger. Did you specify what medical problems you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I had a light stroke on the left-hand side, and after that, I'm suffering from a degree of forgetfulness or I sometimes have a tendency of misspeaking. I have one thing in mind and I say something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Those kind of interpretation issues can be clarified outside the courtroom with the assistance of CLSS, with the assistance of tape. Let's proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Prstojevic, is it also correct that in January of 1992, you became president of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to begin by asking you a few questions about the Serbian Democratic Party which I understand you joined in 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain to the Court, please, the structure of the SDS; that is, whether it was a hierarchical organisation? If so, what body or bodies were at the top, what was the -- what bodies were beneath it and what the nature of the communication was?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I joined the Serbian Democratic Party on St. Peter's day which is the 12th of July, 1990. I became actively involved one month before the November elections in 1990. According to the organisational chart, the top part of the party is actually the Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party. It is a body that has most members, and it is this body that elects all other organs and officials in leading positions in the party. After the Assembly comes the Main Board of the SDS. The Main Board of the SDS has its own Executive Board or a government, as it were. In the city of Sarajevo, there was also a city board. There were municipal boards of the Serbian Democratic Party established in municipalities. And finally, in local communes, we had local boards of the Serbian Democratic Party. Ilidza had a municipal board and 21 local boards of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the local and municipal boards receive instructions or directives from the higher bodies such as the Main Board or Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly did not issue directives. As a rule, this is done on most occasions by the Executive Board or very seldom by the Main Board. As a rule, the municipal boards operate in compliance with the Statute of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the Main Board or the Executive Board -- apart from -- from the municipal boards' efforts to comply with the Statute of the Serbian Democratic Party, did municipal boards receive instructions or directions from the Main Board or Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: One can reply in affirmative, but in the case of Sarajevo, one needs to know that between these two organs, there was also the city board, and that was our main hub for communication and co-operation, and I was a member of the city board of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were municipal boards obliged to implement the directions or instructions issued by the Main Board or Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the municipal boards -- let me ask you about the flow of information up. Did the local boards report to the municipal boards, did the municipal boards report back to the Executive Board and the municipal board about their activities locally?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course that the local boards were responsible to the municipal board, and the municipal board, depending on the requirements and needs, would provide oral or verbal information to the city board, or if there was some need or some directive from the Executive Board of the SDS, it was possible to circumvent the city board and pass it on through a different channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you sometimes in direct contact with -- as president of the Ilidza municipal board, were you sometimes in direct contact with the Executive Board or Main Board?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how frequently did that occur, or did that depend on the particular issue involved?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: That depended on the specific issue, but I would like to emphasise that the president of the Executive Board of the SDS, Mr. Velibor Ostojic, was the resident of Ilidza, i.e., our municipality. Therefore, he was at our disposal without any limitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify, Mr. Prstojevic, is it correct that Mr. Ostojic was the president of the Executive Board until approximately July 1991, and thereafter, at least until the outbreak of the conflict or so, the president of the Executive Board was Mr. Rajko Dukic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about any conflict, but I know that for one part of 1991, Mr. Rajko Dukic was the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry about that. By conflict, that was a synonym for war. It didn't mean a conflict within the party.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but the war was not on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Apart from minor deviations or discrepancies in compliance with directions from the Main Board or Executive Board, was the local leadership permitted not to implement any directions or instructions it received?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Some leaderships implemented things in full. Some did it in part. But there were also some sloppy leaderships.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Apart from inadequate local leaderships, was disobedience to or failure to comply with directions from the party leadership tolerated?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the party leadership often didn't know whether any municipal board carried out something or not. But as far as the Ilidza municipal board is concerned, this was the situation: We would mainly carry out a directive, if we received one. However, if we believed that a segment or certain segments of the directive did not apply to us, or were unnecessary, or were redundant, we would not have carried them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prstojevic, I didn't appreciate that my question was -- would be interpreted by you as referring to the necessity to -- by local boards to interpret what was relevant to them. But my -- let me make that question even more clear: Apart from the obvious aspect of determining what directions or instructions applied to the local municipality, if it was clear it applied to the local leadership, were they duty-bound to implement it and would a failure to implement it be tolerated by the party leadership?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I gave you a specific answer. It was necessary to implement them, but the Ilidza municipal board also didn't implement everything, and did not -- and was not answerable for that to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about something you said previously and ask if that refreshes your recollection or if you can reconcile that for us. On the 14th of June 2005, you were asked, and that's at page 14500: "Did conclusions or directives issued by the Main Boards and transmitted to the municipal and city boards have to be implemented by the local boards or by the municipal and city boards?" And your answer was: "Absolutely. It is clear that it had to be implemented. There might have been minor discrepancies, but in that case it would mean that the local leadership would be disobeying the top leadership and that would not have been tolerated on any occasion." Now, that was testimony in the Krajisnik case, as I mentioned. Was that accurate or not, Mr. Prstojevic, and -- first of all?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's accurate. But I'm going to give you examples of them not implementing any decisions, and I mentioned those examples in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those are the examples you just gave of instructions that were not relevant to the particular locale?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to intervene. The witness did not say who -- the ones that did not refer to the board but ones that are not relevant. They don't -- that don't suit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, that can be clarified later on. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I want to ask you about a particular instruction, and with that in mind I'd like to call up P986, I believe the number is. Of course, I've got the wrong number. That's P960 I apologise to the ... just waiting for the document to come up in English, Mr. Prstojevic. Mr. Prstojevic, in the screen in front of you is a document entitled, "Instructions for the organisation and operations of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in emergency conditions," dated 19 December 1991, with the heading at the top, "Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Main Board." When did -- did officials in Ilidza, Mr. Prstojevic, receive this document from the party leadership?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when and where was that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: We received this document after this date, after the 19th of December, at the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the Holiday Inn Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was the -- when you say you received it at the Assembly, did you receive it at an Assembly session or at the Assembly building or do you recall?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: This was a large gathering. I said a bit earlier that there must have been more than 500 people there, with five people from Ilidza present among them. I don't remember how we got the document, but I know for a fact that it was not discussed at the meeting. There was no discussion about that document at that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was present at that meeting, Mr. Prstojevic? What -- what kind of officials?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was invited to the meeting as the president of the Ilidza Serbian Democratic Party. The president of the Executive Board of the Ilidza municipality, Mr. Radomir Kezunovic; the secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Ilidza, Momcilo Ceklic. The meetings of this kind were always attended by the people's deputy, Ljubo Bosiljcic, and also the commander of the TO staff, Dragan Markovic, was also present. He was also representing the Ilidza municipality. He was an official of the Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what about from other municipalities, Mr. Prstojevic? Were they represented in the same manner?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think so. I assume that in the same way, the other municipalities should have been represented. This kind of meeting is usually attended by specific types of people, specific officials and members, either of the government or the party bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about members of the party leadership? Were they present?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, our top party leaders attended, as well as representatives in the organs of power of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Among them, Mr. Nikola Koljevic and Mrs. Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are those the only two party leaders in attendance whom you can recall?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, was also present. Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, Velibor Ostojic and many others. I don't need to list all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you say or you mentioned that there was no discussion about the document at that session. Let me ask you -- direct your attention to something you said before, see if that refreshes your recollection at all about whether or not there was any discussion. At page 14503, you were discussing the December 19th instructions, and you were asked: "And what was explained to the assembled people at the meeting about the document?" And your answer was: "I can't remember in any great detail because it was a long time ago." And then you went on to talk about the fact that it was partly an Assembly involving some elections and talk about everything that happened: "It is rather difficult to remember what exactly took place in the course of that Assembly because it went on for several hours." Now that seemed to indicate you couldn't recall in detail what was discussed, Mr. Prstojevic. Does that refresh your recollection about whether or not the document was discussed at all during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was clear to me then, and it's even more clear to me now, that the document was not discussed. When you move further, you will see what I said in Mr. Krajisnik's case. I don't know who took the document, at the meeting, or in the hall, or in the corridor or somewhere. That point in the event I did not register. I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did officials in Ilidza, including yourself, consider themselves duty-bound to implement the agreement -- the instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: I personally thought that I should implement this instruction or these instructions, for a number of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what were those reasons?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: When somebody gave me these instructions, when I was in Ilidza, and after I read them, I established that the instructions were drafted on the basis of a book that I do have here with me. It's called, "The strategy of All People's Defence and social self protection in wartime and during immediate danger of war." As an officer, and as a director, and with TO staffs located at each enterprise, and because I was the president of the committee for All People's Defence and social self protection, and also in view of the fact that there was a committee in municipalities for All People's Defence and social self protection, or ONODSZ, the president of the -- that committee is -- the president of the municipality is automatically the president of that committee. All that was practically changed was the name. I could see that. Instead of socialist terminology such as "Komitet," committee, the term Crisis Staff, "Krizni Stab," was used, but the book I'm referring to, the wartime book, recognises staffs, only doesn't refer to them as Crisis Staffs. When the TO staff and the civilian protection staffs are merged, it immediately becomes a committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I'm going to ask you some more questions about what was implemented and what the nature of the document is, but let me ask you quickly: Did Ilidza proceed to implement the instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I remember the time we had to adjourn and it seems it's going to be difficult for me to get into the text of the document in the limited time we have, which is 30 seconds. But I'm in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has been a long day. If necessary --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for this week, and next week we have two witnesses fixed for Tuesday and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For Wednesday and Thursday, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wednesday and Thursday. So we will continue with Mr. Prstojevic on Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you not file a notification correcting the dates that are fixed on 8th and 9th? Could you check it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you'll give me just a moment, Your Honour, I know that part of this was the result of -- or part of our calculations were the result of the confusion about the Monday and Tuesday sitting dates, so I'm not sure if there has been the filing of the document which has been inconsistent with my information while we are in court, let me check on that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While you're checking, I'll hear from Mr. Karadzic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 182 is planned for Tuesday and Wednesday, yes. And after that, we are supposed to continue with Mr. Prstojevic. When should the Defence prepare for the cross-examination of such important witnesses? We are exposed to different kinds of pressure. We can see all the resources that the Prosecution has and still they are encountering problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't follow. I find it difficult to follow. You don't have time to prepare for whom?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both, for both of them. If I have one, then I can prepare well. But if I have two, then it's a large burden; either/or, not both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have more than sufficient time to prepare for cross-examination. They were notified a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, by way of clarification, whatever is before -- I know there were prior pleadings that indicated, I think, a different date but there is no -- I'm advised that the witness to whom we have been referring, and I believe the number is 182, is fixed for Wednesday and Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll continue with Mr. Prstojevic on Tuesday at 9.00. And his evidence -- he will be interposed by Witness 182, not by 354.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps I should check on that. Perhaps both because there is -- I think we have the -- I'd have to check on whether or not we have an additional witness who is also fixed but for a very, very brief time. I have some recollection about that but let me double check on that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, Mr. Prstojevic may be interposed yet again? Tuesday week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just for clarification, the witness I was referring to - and I'm not going to refer to the witness by name, but by the KDZ number - the Court may recall it was a very brief witness whose total allotted time, that's 359, was, I think, an hour and a half for both the direct and cross-examination, and for various reasons, we had fixed that witness for Thursday, but that would have been Wednesday and Thursday, as I mentioned, were already allotted to completing the examination of 182.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prstojevic? What was it that you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been informed that I continue my testimony on the 8th of March of this year, and that before that, there will be other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will hear you on 8th of March, next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And perhaps it's useful to note at this time or at least it perhaps shouldn't be omitted, given the length of cross-examination, it's probably worth noting we have a fixed witness for the week after next week as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe introduce the third shift then, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For planning purpose, probably you may be in the position to indicate to the Chamber how much time you would need for your examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm trying to -- I'll do my best but I'm not in a position to do that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I then know when I am to cross-examine Mr. Prstojevic? Because probably Mr. Tieger would need the whole of Tuesday and perhaps he would need a few more days after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's high mathematics. We will adjourn. Thanks for the indulgence of the interpreters and court reporters and other staff. Everybody have a nice, restful weekend. Tuesday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of March, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.22 p.m.,
